scalar.title: Scalar
scalar.definition: A number, a quantity without direction. Applied mathematics usually works with real $\mathbb{R}$ or complex $\mathbb{C}$ numbers. Also: natural $\mathbb{N}$, integer $\mathbb{Z}$, rational $\mathbb{Q}$.

vector.title: Vector
vector.definition: An ordered list of numbers; can be viewed as a point in $n$-dimensional space or a directed segment. $\vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$. Vectors are added and multiplied by a scalar element-wise.

scalar_product.title: Dot product
scalar_product.definition: The scalar (dot) product of vectors: $\vec{x} \cdot \vec{y} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i$. Used for cosine similarity between vectors (e.g., embeddings).

cosine_similarity.title: Cosine similarity
cosine_similarity.definition: A measure of vector closeness: $\cos(\theta) = \frac{A \cdot B}{\|A\|\|B\|}$. Used to find similar objects by their embeddings. Cosine distance: $d(A, B) = 1 - \cos(\theta)$.

matrix.title: Matrix
matrix.definition: An $m \times n$ table of numbers; matrices can be added (same size), multiplied (compatible dimensions), and transposed ($A^T$). Matrix multiplication is not commutative: $AB \neq BA$. Used for linear transformations.

transpose.title: Transpose
transpose.definition: The operation $A^T$: rows become columns. $a_{ij}^T = a_{ji}$. A symmetric matrix satisfies $A^T = A$.

tensor.title: Tensor
tensor.definition: A generalization of a scalar (order 0), vector (1), and matrix (2) to multidimensional arrays. A tensor of order $k$ has $k$ dimensions. In neural networks, a batch of images is a tensor of shape $[batch, channels, height, width]$.

vector_space.title: Vector space
vector_space.definition: A set with vector addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the axioms of commutativity, associativity, existence of zero, and distributivity. Examples: $\mathbb{R}^n$, embedding spaces.

linear_combination.title: Linear combination
linear_combination.definition: An expression $\vec{u} = \alpha_1 \vec{v}_1 + \dots + \alpha_k \vec{v}_k$. All such combinations form the linear span $\operatorname{span}\{\vec{v}_1, \dots, \vec{v}_k\}$.

basis.title: Basis
basis.definition: A maximal set of linearly independent vectors. The dimension of the space is the number of basis vectors. Any vector decomposes uniquely in the basis; the coefficients are the vector's coordinates.

subspace.title: Subspace
subspace.definition: A subset of a vector space that is itself a vector space. A hyperplane is a subspace of dimension $n-1$ in an $n$-dimensional space.

linear_independence.title: Linear dependence and independence
linear_independence.definition: Vectors are linearly dependent if a nontrivial linear combination equals zero (at least one is expressed through the others). They are linearly independent if only the trivial combination equals zero. A basis is a minimal set of linearly independent vectors that spans the space.

rank.title: Matrix rank
rank.definition: The maximum number of linearly independent rows or columns; $\operatorname{rank}(A) \leq \min(m,n)$. Interpreted as the dimension of the matrix's image. LoRA uses low-rank matrices $\Delta W = AB$.

determinant.title: Determinant
determinant.definition: A scalar $\det A$ for a square matrix: it reflects the volume of a parallelepiped, invertibility ($\det A = 0$ means the matrix is singular), and whether orientation is preserved or flipped. Elementary operations do not change the rank.

eigenvalue.title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
eigenvalue.definition: If $Av = \lambda v$, then $v$ is an eigenvector and $\lambda$ an eigenvalue. The spectrum is the set of all eigenvalues. Used in PCA (principal components are eigenvectors of the covariance matrix).

svd.title: SVD (Singular Value Decomposition)
svd.definition: A matrix decomposition $F = U \Sigma V^T$, where $U$ and $V$ are orthogonal (columns are eigenvectors of $FF^T$ and $F^TF$) and $\Sigma$ is diagonal with singular values. Used for dimensionality reduction, compression, and recommendations.

alg_orthogonality.title: Orthogonality
alg_orthogonality.definition: Vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero, meaning they share no common component. An orthonormal basis provides independent axes of unit length.

alg_inverse_matrix.title: Inverse and singular matrices
alg_inverse_matrix.definition: The inverse matrix recovers the original vector: A⁻¹A = I. It exists only for a nonsingular matrix with a nonzero determinant and full rank.

set.title: Set
set.definition: A collection of objects treated as a whole. $x \in A$ means element $x$ belongs to set $A$. Operations: union $A \cup B$, intersection $A \cap B$, difference $A \setminus B$, complement $\overline{A}$.

function_one_variable.title: Function of One Variable
function_one_variable.definition: A rule $f: X \to Y$ that assigns to each $x \in X$ a unique $y \in Y$. $X$ is the domain, $Y$ the codomain. Elementary functions: power, exponential, logarithmic, trigonometric, and their inverses.

function_several_variables.title: Function of Several Variables
function_several_variables.definition: A mapping $y = f(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ from a domain $D \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}$. In ML, loss functions and models often depend on many parameters (weights).

composition.title: Composition
composition.definition: Sequential application: $(g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x))$. For matrices, composing linear maps is matrix multiplication $C = AB$ (first $B$, then $A$).

limit.title: Limit
limit.definition: The number $L$ that a sequence $x_n$ approaches as $n \to \infty$: $\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = L$. The limit of a function at a point is the value $f(x)$ approaches as $x \to x_0$.

continuity.title: Continuity
continuity.definition: A function is continuous at $x_0$ if $\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = f(x_0)$, i.e., it has no jumps. In ML, loss functions (e.g., MSE) should be continuous for gradients to be computed correctly.

derivative.title: Derivative
derivative.definition: The derivative $f'(x)$ is the limit of the ratio of the function's increment to the argument's increment as $\Delta x \to 0$. It shows the function's rate of change. Rules: sum, product, quotient, power function.

partial_derivative.title: Partial Derivative
partial_derivative.definition: The derivative of a function of several variables with respect to one variable, holding the others fixed. Used for gradients and backpropagation in ML.

approximation.title: Function Approximation
approximation.definition: Approximating a function with another, simpler or more convenient one. Taylor and Fourier series; a neural network is a universal approximator (Cybenko's theorem).

smooth_function.title: Smooth Function
smooth_function.definition: A function with a continuous first derivative ($f \in C^1$). MSE is a smooth loss function; non-smoothness can hinder gradient-based optimization.

extremum.title: Extremum
extremum.definition: A maximum or minimum of a function. Local: within a neighborhood of a point; global: over the whole domain. In ML we minimize the loss function, and local minima are possible.

gradient.title: Gradient
gradient.definition: The vector of partial derivatives $\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = (\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}, \dots, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n})^T$. Points in the direction of steepest ascent; used in ML for gradient descent.

norm.title: Vector Norm
norm.definition: The "length" of a vector. The $L_p$ norm: $\|x\|_p = (\sum |x_i|^p)^{1/p}$. $L_1$ is the Manhattan norm (LASSO), $L_2$ the Euclidean norm (Ridge). The unit circle looks different for different norms.

calc_chain_rule.title: Chain Rule
calc_chain_rule.definition: The derivative of a composition is the product of derivatives: (f(g(x)))' = f'(g(x))·g'(x). Backpropagation in neural networks is built on it.

calc_hessian.title: Hessian
calc_hessian.definition: The matrix of second partial derivatives. Its eigenvalues distinguish a minimum, a maximum, and a saddle point; in deep learning computing it in full is too expensive.

calc_jacobian.title: Jacobian
calc_jacobian.definition: The matrix of first partial derivatives of a vector-valued function $f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$: $J_{ij} = \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}$, of size $m \times n$. For $m = 1$ it reduces to the gradient (a row). Not to be confused with the Hessian, which consists of second derivatives of a scalar function.

calc_convexity.title: Convexity
calc_convexity.definition: A function is convex if the segment between any two points of its graph lies on or above the graph. A convex function has a unique local minimum, which is also global, so optimization is easy.

calc_argmin_argmax.title: argmin and argmax
calc_argmin_argmax.definition: Not the value of a function but the point where it is attained: argmin is the argument of the minimum, argmax of the maximum. Training a model is written as the argmin of the loss function over the parameters.

kl_divergence.title: KL Divergence
kl_divergence.definition: A measure of how one probability distribution differs from another: $D_{KL}(p \| q) = \sum p(x) \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}$. Not symmetric; used as the loss in soft-label distillation (the student approaches the teacher's distribution), while MiniLLM uses reverse KL. In ML, KL is often minimized for compression or knowledge transfer.

random_variable.title: Random Variable
random_variable.definition: A discrete one takes a finite or countable set of values with given probabilities. A continuous one takes any value in an interval and is described by a density. Examples: number of calls (discrete), a person's height (continuous).

probability_function.title: Probability Mass Function
probability_function.definition: For a discrete random variable $\xi$, gives $\mathbb{P}(\xi = x)$. The values sum to 1 over all $x$, each lies in $[0, 1]$. Describes the distribution of a discrete variable.

density.title: Probability Density
density.definition: A function $f(x) \geq 0$ for a continuous random variable with $\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(x)\, dx = 1$. The probability of landing in $[a,b]$ is $\int_a^b f(x)\, dx$. Note: $f(x)$ itself is not a probability but an "intensity".

normal_distribution.title: Normal Distribution
normal_distribution.definition: A continuous distribution with density $f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}$. Parameters: $\mu$ is the expected value (also median and mode), $\sigma^2$ is the variance. Standard normal: $\mu=0$, $\sigma=1$. Examples: height, IQ, measurement errors.

exponential_distribution.title: Exponential Distribution
exponential_distribution.definition: A continuous distribution with density $f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x \geq 0$ and $0$ for $x < 0$. Models the time until an event (failure, call, customer arrival).

bernoulli.title: Bernoulli Distribution
bernoulli.definition: A discrete random variable with two outcomes: $1$ with probability $p$ and $0$ with probability $1-p$. Models a single trial (success/failure): a click, a purchase, a hit.

poisson.title: Poisson Distribution
poisson.definition: A discrete distribution: $\mathbb{P}(Y=k) = \frac{\lambda^k}{k!} e^{-\lambda}$. Models the number of events in a fixed interval: calls, visitors, typos.

expectation.title: Expected Value
expectation.definition: The average outcome over many samples, $\mathbb{E}\xi$. Discrete: $\sum a_i p_i$; continuous: $\int x f(x)\, dx$. Reflects the "expected" result of an experiment.

variance.title: Variance
variance.definition: A measure of spread of a random variable: $\mathbb{D}\xi = \mathbb{E}(\xi - \mathbb{E}\xi)^2 = \mathbb{E}\xi^2 - (\mathbb{E}\xi)^2$. The larger the variance, the more the values are spread out.

standard_deviation.title: Standard Deviation
standard_deviation.definition: The square root of the variance: $\sigma = \sqrt{\mathbb{D}\xi}$. Measured in the same units as the data, so it is easier to interpret than variance.

joint_probability.title: Joint Probability
joint_probability.definition: $P(A, B)$ is the probability that both events $A$ and $B$ occur. For independent events: $P(A,B) = P(A)P(B)$; for dependent ones: $P(A,B) = P(B)P(A|B)$.

conditional_probability.title: Conditional Probability
conditional_probability.definition: The probability of $A$ given $B$: $P(A \mid B) = P(A, B) / P(B)$. Shows how knowing $B$ changes the probability of $A$. Under independence, $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$.

bayes_theorem.title: Bayes' Theorem
bayes_theorem.definition: A formula for updating a probability after a new observation: $P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A) P(A)}{P(B)}$. Used in the naive Bayes classifier and Bayesian inference.

proba_correlation.title: Correlation
proba_correlation.definition: A measure of linear association between two variables, from −1 to 1 (Pearson coefficient); Spearman's rank correlation captures monotonic relationships. Correlation does not imply causation.

proba_covariance.title: Covariance and Covariance Matrix
proba_covariance.definition: Covariance shows how two variables deviate together; its value depends on scale, so it is normalized into correlation. The covariance matrix collects all pairs of features.

proba_entropy.title: Entropy and Cross-Entropy
proba_entropy.definition: Entropy is the average uncertainty of a distribution, in bits or nats. Cross-entropy measures the cost of encoding the true distribution with the predicted one and serves as the classification loss.

proba_clt.title: CLT (Central Limit Theorem)
proba_clt.definition: The sum or mean of many independent, identically distributed variables approaches a normal distribution. The justification for z-tests and confidence intervals for the mean.

population.title: Population
population.definition: All the objects of interest in the context of a problem. Usually studied through a sample, since examining every object is impossible or expensive.

sample_stats.title: Sample (in statistics)
sample_stats.definition: A subset of the population used to draw conclusions. It can be representative or unrepresentative. Denoted $X$ or $x_1, \dots, x_n$.

sample_mean.title: Sample Mean
sample_mean.definition: An estimate of the mean from a sample: $\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$. Sensitive to outliers.

sample_variance.title: Sample Variance
sample_variance.definition: An estimate of the variance from a sample: $s^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2$. The unbiased estimate uses the divisor $n-1$ instead of $n$.

mode_stats.title: Mode
mode_stats.definition: The value that occurs most often in a sample. Distributions can be unimodal or multimodal (bimodal, etc.).

median_stats.title: Median
median_stats.definition: The value that splits an ordered sample in half. Less sensitive to outliers than the mean. For odd $n$ it is the middle element; for even $n$, the average of the two middle ones.

bootstrap.title: Bootstrap
bootstrap.definition: A method for estimating the distribution of a statistic by repeatedly resampling the original data with replacement. Lets you build confidence intervals and estimate uncertainty without assumptions about the form of the distribution.

statistical_hypothesis.title: Statistical Hypothesis
statistical_hypothesis.definition: An assumption about a distribution or its parameters. $H_0$ is the null hypothesis, $H_1$ the alternative. A test lets you reject or fail to reject $H_0$ based on data (often via the $p$-value).

confidence_interval.title: Confidence Interval
confidence_interval.definition: An interval that contains an unknown population parameter with a given confidence (e.g., 95%). Built from a sample; interpreted as the plausible range for the true parameter.

type_i_ii_error.title: Type I and Type II Errors
type_i_ii_error.definition: Type I error: rejecting $H_0$ when it is true (false alarm, False Positive). Type II error: failing to reject $H_0$ when $H_1$ is true (miss, False Negative). $\alpha$ is the significance level, $1-\beta$ is the test's power.

parametric_nonparametric.title: Parametric and Nonparametric Tests
parametric_nonparametric.definition: Parametric tests assume the form of the distribution (often normality), e.g., Student's $t$-test. Nonparametric tests do not (Mann–Whitney, Wilcoxon). Parametric tests are more powerful when their assumptions hold; nonparametric ones are more robust to outliers.

t_test.title: t-test (Student's)
t_test.definition: A test for comparing the means of two samples; it checks whether the difference is statistically significant. Used for small samples under a normality assumption. There are independent and paired $t$-tests.

stat_ab_test.title: A/B Test
stat_ab_test.definition: Comparing two variants on randomly split groups of users. The metric, MDE, significance level, and sample size are fixed in advance; otherwise the result cannot be interpreted.

stat_quantile.title: Quantile and Percentile
stat_quantile.definition: The quantile of level q is the value below which a fraction q of observations lies; a percentile is the same in percent. Robust latency metrics like p95 and p99 are built on them.

stat_iqr.title: Quartiles and IQR
stat_iqr.definition: Quartiles split a sample into four parts; IQR = Q3 − Q1 is the interquartile range. The 1.5·IQR rule flags outliers and draws the box plot's whiskers.

stat_alpha.title: Significance Level α
stat_alpha.definition: The pre-chosen acceptable probability of a Type I error, i.e., rejecting a true null hypothesis. Usually 0.05; the p-value is compared against it.

stat_p_value.title: p-value
stat_p_value.definition: The probability of seeing data at least as extreme as the observed data if the null hypothesis is true. It is neither the probability of the hypothesis nor the effect size.

stat_power.title: Statistical Power
stat_power.definition: The probability of detecting an effect if it really exists (1 − β). Grows with sample size and effect size; low power is a source of false-negative conclusions.

stat_std_error.title: Standard Error
stat_std_error.definition: The standard deviation of a sample estimate: it shows how much the sample mean varies from sample to sample. Decreases as the square root of the sample size and sets the width of the confidence interval.

overfitting.title: Overfitting
overfitting.definition: When a model fits the training set too closely and generalizes poorly to new data. Typical of overly complex models or small datasets.

underfitting.title: Underfitting
underfitting.definition: When a model is too simple to capture the patterns in the data. Quality is low on both the training and the test set.

bias.title: Bias
bias.definition: A model's systematic error: how far its predictions deviate from the truth on average. High bias often comes with underfitting.

ml_variance_spread.title: Variance
ml_variance_spread.definition: How much a model's predictions change when the training set changes. High variance often comes with overfitting.

cross-validation.title: Cross-validation
cross-validation.definition: A way to estimate model quality: the data is split into parts (folds), and the model is trained on some and evaluated on the others in turn. Reduces dependence on a single train/test split.

regularization.title: Regularization
regularization.definition: Adding a penalty for model complexity (e.g., L1/L2 in linear models) to reduce overfitting and improve generalization. In DL it also includes BatchNorm, Dropout, augmentation, etc.

dataset.title: Dataset (sample)
dataset.definition: A subset of data used to train and evaluate ML models, usually a table or array of features and labels. It is split into training, validation, and test sets.

ml.title: Machine Learning
ml.definition: The field of building algorithms that let computers improve their behavior from data (experience) without being explicitly programmed.

classification.title: Classification
classification.definition: An ML task where an object must be assigned to one of a predefined set of discrete classes (binary, multiclass, multilabel).

regression.title: Regression
regression.definition: The task of predicting a numeric (continuous) value from features. The output is $Y = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{R}^m$. Examples: price, temperature, sales volume.

loss.title: Loss Function
loss.definition: A mapping from an algorithm's output to a number: the "cost" of the error on a single object. Depends on the prediction and the true label. Examples: MSE, log loss, cross-entropy.

empirical_risk.title: Empirical Risk
empirical_risk.definition: The algorithm's average error on the training set. Empirical risk minimization picks the algorithm that minimizes this average error and can lead to overfitting.

holdout.title: Hold-out
holdout.definition: A simple split of the data into training and test (and optionally validation) sets. The basic model evaluation scheme.

stratification.title: Stratification
stratification.definition: Splitting into train and test while preserving the class proportions of the original dataset. In sklearn, the stratify parameter. Important for imbalanced classes.

kfold.title: k-Fold
kfold.definition: A cross-validation method: the dataset is split into $k$ parts (folds) and $k$ iterations are run, with each fold serving as the test set once and the rest as training data. A more reliable estimate than hold-out.

bagging.title: Bagging
bagging.definition: An ensemble method: many base learners are trained independently and in parallel on random subsamples of the data, and their outputs are averaged (voting). Reduces variance.

random_forest.title: Random Forest
random_forest.definition: An ensemble of decision trees built on random subsamples of the training data. Each tree is usually shallow; the prediction is an average or a vote. Reduces variance.

boosting.title: Boosting
boosting.definition: An ensemble method: base learners are built sequentially, each one reducing the error of its predecessors. Unlike bagging, training is sequential. Reduces bias.

gradient_boosting.title: Gradient Boosting
gradient_boosting.definition: Boosting in which each new model is trained on the residual errors (loss gradients) of the previous ones. Base models are usually decision trees. XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost.

bias_variance_tradeoff.title: Bias–Variance Trade-off
bias_variance_tradeoff.definition: The compromise between bias and variance: as model complexity grows, bias falls and variance rises. Test error follows a U-shaped curve; moderate complexity is optimal.

sigmoid.title: Sigmoid
sigmoid.definition: The function $\sigma(x) = 1/(1+e^{-x})$, which maps any number to the interval $(0, 1)$. Used for probabilistic outputs (logistic regression, binary classification).

logistic_regression.title: Logistic Regression
logistic_regression.definition: A classification algorithm: the prediction is a class probability given by $\sigma(wx+b)$. The output is in $[0,1]$; the threshold is tuned to the metric. Despite the name, it is a classifier, not a regression.

multicollinearity.title: Multicollinearity
multicollinearity.definition: Strong linear dependence between features (predictors). It makes coefficients harder to interpret and can make estimates unstable in linear and logistic regression. Remedies: feature selection, regularization, PCA.

dimensionality_reduction.title: Dimensionality Reduction
dimensionality_reduction.definition: Transforming data from a high-dimensional space into a lower-dimensional one while preserving structure or variance. Methods: PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, MDS. Used for visualization, denoising, and faster training.

decision_tree.title: Decision Tree
decision_tree.definition: A classification or regression algorithm: a hierarchy of nodes with threshold conditions on features and leaves holding answers. Built using a splitting criterion (entropy, Gini). Prone to overfitting without regularization.

splitting_criterion.title: Splitting Criterion
splitting_criterion.definition: A function that scores the quality of a split at a decision tree node. The feature and threshold are chosen to maximize information gain or minimize impurity. Examples: entropy, Gini, MSE for regression.

clustering.title: Clustering
clustering.definition: An unsupervised learning task: partition objects into groups (clusters) so that objects within a cluster are similar and objects in different clusters differ. Methods: KMeans, DBSCAN, hierarchical, spectral.

kmeans.title: KMeans
kmeans.definition: A clustering algorithm: the data is split into $k$ clusters by minimizing the sum of squared distances from points to cluster centers. Centroids and point assignments are recomputed iteratively. Requires choosing $k$.

dbscan.title: DBSCAN
dbscan.definition: A density-based clustering algorithm: finds clusters of arbitrary shape, groups points in dense regions, and marks outliers as noise. Parameters: radius $\varepsilon$ and $minPts$. No need to set the number of clusters.

unsupervised_learning.title: Unsupervised Learning
unsupervised_learning.definition: A type of machine learning with no labels: the algorithm finds structure in the data on its own. Tasks: clustering, dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection, density estimation.

cluster.title: Cluster
cluster.definition: A group of objects in a clustering task, united by similarity (proximity in feature space or density). Objects within a cluster are similar; objects in different clusters differ.

dendrogram.title: Dendrogram
dendrogram.definition: A tree diagram of hierarchical clustering: the vertical axis shows the distance (or similarity) at which clusters are merged. Cutting it at a given height yields a partition into clusters.

knn.title: KNN (k-Nearest Neighbors)
knn.definition: A lazy classification or regression algorithm: the prediction for an object is based on its $k$ nearest examples in the training set (a class vote or the mean value). The distance is usually Euclidean or Manhattan.

svm.title: Support Vector Machine (SVM)
svm.definition: A classification (and regression) algorithm: finds the separating hyperplane with the maximum margin between classes. Support vectors are the objects on the margin boundary. The kernel trick enables nonlinear boundaries (RBF, polynomial kernel).

pca.title: PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
pca.definition: A dimensionality reduction method: a linear projection of the data onto orthogonal directions of maximum variance. The components are eigenvectors of the covariance matrix. Preserves global structure but loses some information.

tsne.title: t-SNE
tsne.definition: A nonlinear dimensionality reduction method for visualization: preserves local distances between points and models similarity with a Student's t-distribution. Good for 2D/3D visualization; sensitive to perplexity.

umap.title: UMAP
umap.definition: A dimensionality reduction method based on manifold approximation: builds a nearest-neighbor graph and approximates it in a lower-dimensional space. Preserves both local and global structure, is faster than t-SNE, and scales to large data.

ml_hyperparameter.title: Hyperparameter
ml_hyperparameter.definition: A parameter set before training and not learned by gradient descent: tree depth, learning rate, regularization strength. Tuned on validation via search or Bayesian optimization.

ml_precision_recall.title: Precision and Recall
ml_precision_recall.definition: Precision is the share of correct predictions among predicted positives; recall is the share of actual positives that were found. Raising one usually lowers the other, so both are tracked.

ml_accuracy.title: Accuracy
ml_accuracy.definition: The share of correctly classified objects. Misleading on imbalanced data: always predicting the majority class gives high accuracy with zero usefulness.

ml_f1.title: F1 Score
ml_f1.definition: The harmonic mean of precision and recall: one metric instead of two. F-beta shifts the balance: beta > 1 favors recall, beta < 1 favors precision.

ml_roc_auc.title: ROC-AUC
ml_roc_auc.definition: The area under the ROC curve: the probability that a random positive object gets a higher score than a random negative one. Threshold-independent, but optimistic under strong class imbalance.

ml_pr_auc.title: PR-AUC (Precision-Recall Curve)
ml_pr_auc.definition: The area under the precision–recall curve. With a rare positive class it is more informative than ROC-AUC because it does not reward easily guessing negatives.

ml_confusion_matrix.title: Confusion Matrix
ml_confusion_matrix.definition: A table of TP, FP, FN, and TN: how many objects of each class the model assigned where. Precision, recall, and all derived metrics come from it.

ml_regression_metrics.title: MSE, RMSE, and MAE
ml_regression_metrics.definition: Regression metrics: MSE is the mean squared error, RMSE is its square root in the units of the target, MAE is the mean absolute error. MAE is more robust to outliers; MSE penalizes large misses more heavily.

ml_r2.title: R² (Coefficient of Determination)
ml_r2.definition: The share of the target's variance explained by the model: 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than predicting the mean, negative values are worse than the mean.

ml_outlier.title: Outlier
ml_outlier.definition: An observation that sharply deviates from the overall distribution. Detected with the 1.5·IQR rule or a z-score; do not remove blindly, since it may be a rare but genuine event.

ml_data_leakage.title: Data Leakage
ml_data_leakage.definition: Information that is unavailable at prediction time ending up in the features: future values, aggregates over the whole dataset, the target itself. Produces great validation scores and failure in production.

ml_calibration.title: Probability Calibration
ml_calibration.definition: Turning output scores into honest probabilities: among objects scored 0.7, about 70% should be positive. Done with Platt scaling or isotonic regression.

ml_class_imbalance.title: Class Imbalance
ml_class_imbalance.definition: A strong skew in class proportions. Addressed with error weighting, stratification, threshold tuning, oversampling (SMOTE), or undersampling; accuracy becomes useless.

ml_feature_scaling.title: Feature Scaling
ml_feature_scaling.definition: Bringing features to comparable scales: StandardScaler to zero mean and unit variance, MinMaxScaler to a fixed range. Needed for linear models, KNN, and neural networks, but not for trees.

ml_feature_selection.title: Feature Selection
ml_feature_selection.definition: Reducing the feature set to the useful ones: by model importance, by correlation with the target, or stepwise (RFE, RFECV). Reduces overfitting, speeds up training, and simplifies maintenance.

ml_eda.title: EDA (Exploratory Data Analysis)
ml_eda.definition: The first stage of working with data: distributions, missing values, outliers, relationships between features and the target. Generates hypotheses for preprocessing and catches problems before training.

ml_target_encoding.title: Target Encoding
ml_target_encoding.definition: Encoding a category by the mean value of the target. Powerful for high-cardinality categories but leaks easily, so it is computed on an out-of-fold split.

ml_stacking.title: Stacking and Blending
ml_stacking.definition: A second-level ensemble: a meta-model learns from out-of-fold predictions of base models. Blending is the same idea using a holdout set instead of cross-validation.

mlp.title: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP)
mlp.definition: A class of neural networks made of several layers of neurons: an input layer, hidden layers (weights + activation functions), and an output layer. Each neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs + bias + activation (ReLU, sigmoid, etc.).

activation.title: Activation Function
activation.definition: A nonlinear transformation of a neuron's output. It lets the network model nonlinear relationships; without it, a stack of layers is still linear. Examples: ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, GELU.

backpropagation.title: Backpropagation
backpropagation.definition: An algorithm for efficiently computing the gradients of the loss with respect to all network weights (chain rule). The forward pass yields the output and loss, the backward pass yields gradients; then weights are updated by gradient descent.

optimizer.title: Optimizer
optimizer.definition: An algorithm that updates network parameters to minimize the loss. SGD uses the mini-batch gradient; variants include Adam, AdamW, RMSprop, etc., often with momentum and an adaptive step size.

sgd.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)
sgd.definition: In practice usually means mini-batch gradient descent: the gradient is computed on a random subset of samples and the weights are updated. A trade-off between speed and stability.

ema.title: Exponential Moving Average (EMA)
ema.definition: Smoothing of a sequence: $e_t = \beta e_{t-1} + (1-\beta) x_t$. The basis of many optimizers (momentum, Adam). Reduces gradient noise.

weight_initialization.title: Weight Initialization
weight_initialization.definition: Setting initial weight values before training. Convergence and stability depend on it. Options: Xavier (Glorot) for sigmoid/tanh, He for ReLU.

skip_connection.title: Skip Connection (Residual Connection)
skip_connection.definition: Passing an input directly to a deeper layer, bypassing intermediate ones. The output is added to or concatenated with the layers' output. ResNet: $y = F(x)+x$; eases training of deep networks and reduces vanishing gradients.

data_augmentation.title: Data Augmentation
data_augmentation.definition: Artificially enlarging the training set with modified examples (rotations and flips for images; paraphrasing for text). Reduces overfitting and improves generalization.

embedding.title: Embedding
embedding.definition: A fixed-size vector representation of an object (word, image, user); semantically similar objects get nearby vectors. Used in neural networks and for vector search.

attention.title: Attention
attention.definition: A mechanism that lets the model, at each step, pick out and weight the relevant parts of the input (e.g., different positions in a sequence). Queries $Q$, keys $K$, values $V$; the weights come from matching $Q$ against $K$.

transformer.title: Transformer
transformer.definition: A neural network architecture (Attention Is All You Need): attention over sequences without RNNs or convolutions. Processes positions in parallel; encoder-decoder or encoder-only. The basis of BERT, GPT, and others.

dropout.title: Dropout
dropout.definition: Regularization: during training, a random subset of neurons is "switched off" (their output is zeroed with a given probability). Reduces overfitting and keeps the network from relying on individual neurons.

batchnorm.title: Batch Normalization
batchnorm.definition: Normalizing activations over a mini-batch: for each feature, the batch mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$ are computed, values are shifted to $0$ and $1$, then scaled and shifted (learnable). Stabilizes training and allows a higher learning rate.

layernorm.title: Layer Normalization
layernorm.definition: Per-layer normalization: for each sample in the batch, all features are normalized (mean $0$, variance $1$), then scaled and shifted. Common in transformers. Unlike BatchNorm, it does not depend on batch size.

encoder.title: Encoder
encoder.definition: The part of a model that maps the input to an internal representation (hidden states). In a transformer, a stack of layers with self-attention and an FFN; in encoder-decoder models, the decoder uses the encoder's output.

decoder.title: Decoder
decoder.definition: The part of a model that generates the output from the internal representation (and optionally from previous outputs). In a transformer, a stack of layers with masked self-attention, cross-attention to the encoder, and an FFN.

lstm.title: LSTM
lstm.definition: Long Short-Term Memory, an RNN variant with a memory cell and gates (forget, input, output). Mitigates vanishing gradients and can capture long-range dependencies.

gru.title: GRU
gru.definition: Gated Recurrent Unit, a simplified gated RNN (reset, update gates). Fewer parameters than LSTM with often comparable quality. Used for sequences.

rnn.title: RNN
rnn.definition: Recurrent neural network: processes sequences, with a state that depends on the previous step. The vanilla version suffers from vanishing gradients; LSTM and GRU are improved variants.

elu.title: ELU
elu.definition: Exponential Linear Unit: $\text{ELU}(x)=x$ for $x>0$ and $\alpha(e^{x}-1)$ for $x\le 0$. A smooth negative part that can speed up convergence compared with ReLU.

augmentation_short.title: Augmentation
augmentation_short.definition: Artificially expanding the training set by transforming examples (rotations, flips, noise for images; paraphrasing for text). Reduces overfitting and improves generalization.

exploding_gradients.title: Exploding Gradients
exploding_gradients.definition: A sharp growth of gradient norms during backpropagation in deep networks (e.g., RNNs). Causes instability and NaNs. Fixes: gradient clipping, normalization, proper initialization.

vanishing_gradients.title: Vanishing Gradients
vanishing_gradients.definition: Gradients become tiny as they flow backward, so early layers barely learn. Typical for long RNNs and very deep networks. Fixes: ReLU, skip connections, LSTM/GRU.

pooling.title: Pooling
pooling.definition: Downsampling a feature map: over a window (e.g., $2\times 2$) take the maximum (max pooling) or the mean (average pooling). Shrinks spatial size and adds invariance to small shifts.

convolution.title: Convolution
convolution.definition: The core operation of convolutional networks: a kernel (filter) slides over the input, computing a dot product at each position. Extracts local patterns (edges, textures). The basis of CNNs for images and beyond.

warmup.title: Warm-up
warmup.definition: An initial training phase in which the learning rate is increased linearly (or by another schedule) from zero or a small value to its target. Reduces instability early in training.

scheduler.title: Scheduler
scheduler.definition: A learning rate scheduler: changes the learning rate by step or epoch (step decay, cosine annealing, plateau). Used alongside the optimizer for better convergence.

finetuning.title: Fine-tuning
finetuning.definition: Further training of a pretrained model on a target dataset or task, usually with a lower learning rate and sometimes with some layers frozen. Saves data and compute.

pretraining.title: Pretraining
pretraining.definition: Training a model on a large task or dataset (often self-supervised or on a different task) to learn useful representations. The model is then fine-tuned on the target task.

finetuning_ru.title: Further Training
finetuning_ru.definition: Training an already trained (e.g., pretrained) model on new data or a new task. Essentially a synonym for fine-tuning.

model_weights.title: Model Weights
model_weights.definition: The parameters of a neural network (weight and bias matrices and vectors) that are updated during training. Their initialization and scale affect convergence and stability.

logits.title: Logits
logits.definition: The raw continuous values a model outputs before an activation function is applied.

dl_softmax.title: Softmax
dl_softmax.definition: Turns a vector of logits into a probability distribution: the exponential of each value divided by their sum. It is shift-invariant, so the maximum is subtracted from the logits for numerical stability.

dl_learning_rate.title: Learning Rate
dl_learning_rate.definition: The optimizer's step size. Too large causes divergence and loss spikes; too small means slow training and getting stuck. In practice it follows a schedule with warm-up.

dl_cross_entropy.title: Cross-Entropy
dl_cross_entropy.definition: The standard classification loss: the negative log-probability of the correct class. Heavily penalizes confident mistakes and gives well-conditioned gradients when paired with softmax.

dl_adam.title: Adam and AdamW
dl_adam.definition: Adaptive optimizers: Adam keeps moving averages of the gradient and its square; AdamW decouples weight decay from the adaptive step and is the default for transformers.

dl_mixed_precision.title: Mixed Precision (fp16 / bf16)
dl_mixed_precision.definition: Training where weights are stored in fp32 while computation runs in 16 bits: half the memory and faster matrix ops. bf16 has a wider range; fp16 requires loss scaling.

dl_epoch.title: Epoch, Iteration, Step
dl_epoch.definition: An epoch is one full pass over the training set; an iteration (step) is one weight update on a batch. Steps per epoch equal the dataset size divided by the batch size.

dl_batch_size.title: Batch Size
dl_batch_size.definition: How many examples are processed per weight update. A larger batch gives a more stable gradient and better GPU utilization but needs more memory and usually a larger learning rate.

dl_positional_encoding.title: Positional Encoding
dl_positional_encoding.definition: A way to tell a transformer the token order, which attention alone cannot see: sinusoids, learned position embeddings, or relative schemes such as RoPE and ALiBi.

dl_weight_decay.title: Weight Decay
dl_weight_decay.definition: A penalty on large weights, equivalent to L2 regularization, that keeps the model from overfitting. In AdamW it is applied directly to the weights rather than through the loss gradient.

dl_early_stopping.title: Early Stopping
dl_early_stopping.definition: Stopping training once the validation metric has not improved for a set number of epochs. A cheap guard against overfitting; usually the best checkpoint is restored, not the last one.

dl_multi_head_attention.title: Multi-Head Attention
dl_multi_head_attention.definition: Attention computed in parallel by several heads in lower-dimensional subspaces. Different heads capture different dependencies; their outputs are concatenated.

dl_gradient_clipping.title: Gradient Clipping
dl_gradient_clipping.definition: Capping the gradient norm before the optimizer step. Keeps rare huge gradients from wrecking the weights; essential for RNNs and LLM training.

dl_gradient_accumulation.title: Gradient Accumulation
dl_gradient_accumulation.definition: Accumulating gradients over several micro-batches before a weight update: the effect of a large batch when GPU memory is short, at the cost of proportionally longer steps.

dl_gradient_checkpointing.title: Gradient Checkpointing
dl_gradient_checkpointing.definition: Trading compute for memory: intermediate activations are not stored but recomputed during the backward pass. Saves GPU memory while slowing each step by roughly a third.

dl_label_smoothing.title: Label Smoothing
dl_label_smoothing.definition: Replacing the hard target 1 with a slightly softened distribution. Reduces overconfidence, improves calibration, and often slightly boosts validation quality.

dl_parallelism.title: Training Parallelism (DDP, FSDP, ZeRO)
dl_parallelism.definition: Ways to distribute training: data parallelism copies the model across GPUs and splits the batch, tensor and pipeline parallelism split the model itself, and FSDP and ZeRO additionally shard weights and optimizer states.

dl_transfer_learning.title: Transfer Learning
dl_transfer_learning.definition: Reusing a pretrained model's knowledge for a new task: its head is replaced and it is fine-tuned fully or partially. Drastically reduces the amount of labeled data needed.

dl_conv_params.title: Stride, Padding, and Kernel Size
dl_conv_params.definition: Convolution parameters: kernel size sets the window, stride sets the step and how much the map shrinks, and padding adds zeros around the edges to preserve size.

dl_receptive_field.title: Receptive Field
dl_receptive_field.definition: The region of the input image that affects one neuron in a deep layer. It grows with depth, kernel size, and stride, and determines the scale of objects the network can see.

dl_contrastive.title: Contrastive Learning
dl_contrastive.definition: Learning representations by pulling similar pairs together and pushing dissimilar ones apart (InfoNCE, triplet loss). Works without labels and underpins embedding models for search.

cv_image_matrix.title: Image as a pixel matrix
cv_image_matrix.definition: A digital image is a two-dimensional array of intensity values; a color image adds a third axis for channels. All filters and convolutions operate on this array.

cv_rgb.title: RGB and color channels
cv_rgb.definition: A model where color is composed of red, green, and blue channels. Each channel is a separate intensity matrix; a neural network receives them as three input channels.

cv_hsv.title: HSV
cv_hsv.definition: A "hue, saturation, value" color space. It separates color from illumination, so color-based threshold segmentation is more robust in HSV than in RGB.

cv_grayscale.title: Grayscale image
cv_grayscale.definition: A single-channel image that stores only intensity. Cuts memory and compute threefold where color is not needed: edge detection, text recognition.

cv_bit_depth.title: Bit depth
cv_bit_depth.definition: The number of bits per channel: 8 bits give 256 levels, 16 bits give 65,536. Greater depth means finer tones and less banding in gradients, but more data.

cv_kernel.title: Filter kernel (mask)
cv_kernel.definition: A small matrix of weights slid across the image, computing a weighted sum of neighboring pixels at each position. The weights determine the effect: blur, sharpening, edges.

cv_gaussian_blur.title: Gaussian blur
cv_gaussian_blur.definition: Convolution with a Gaussian kernel: averages neighboring pixels with weights following a normal distribution. Suppresses noise before edge detection but also smears the edges themselves.

cv_median_filter.title: Median filter
cv_median_filter.definition: A nonlinear filter: each pixel is replaced by the median of its neighborhood. Unlike averaging, it removes salt-and-pepper impulse noise well while preserving edges.

cv_sobel.title: Sobel operator
cv_sobel.definition: A pair of convolution kernels approximating the intensity derivatives in x and y. Their magnitude gives an edge map, a basic step in many classical detectors.

cv_gabor.title: Gabor filter
cv_gabor.definition: A sinusoid under a Gaussian envelope: it responds to texture of a given frequency and orientation. Used as a handcrafted counterpart of the first convolutional layers.

cv_noise.title: Image noise
cv_noise.definition: Random deviations of intensity from the true value: Gaussian noise from the sensor, salt-and-pepper impulse noise from transmission errors. Different noise types call for different filters.

cv_dft.title: DFT (Discrete Fourier Transform)
cv_dft.definition: Decomposes an image into sinusoids of different frequencies, yielding a spectrum with amplitude and phase. Enables frequency filtering and analysis of periodic structures.

cv_dct.title: DCT (Discrete Cosine Transform)
cv_dct.definition: A relative of the Fourier transform with real coefficients that concentrates energy in low frequencies. JPEG compression is built on it: high frequencies are simply discarded.

cv_frequency_domain.title: Frequency domain (spectrum)
cv_frequency_domain.definition: Representing an image through frequencies: low frequencies carry the overall background and smooth transitions, high frequencies carry edges, texture, and noise.

cv_affine.title: Affine transformation
cv_affine.definition: A linear transformation plus a translation: rotation, scaling, shift, shear. Preserves parallel lines; defined by a 2×3 matrix and requires interpolation when resampling pixels.

cv_interpolation.title: Interpolation
cv_interpolation.definition: Computing a pixel value at fractional coordinates during rotation or scaling: nearest neighbor, bilinear, bicubic, from fast and coarse to smooth and slow.

cv_homography.title: Homography
cv_homography.definition: A 3×3 matrix relating two planes across different shots of a scene. Used to align frames when stitching panoramas and to correct perspective.

cv_ransac.title: RANSAC
cv_ransac.definition: Robust model estimation from data with outliers: a random minimal subset is sampled repeatedly, and the hypothesis with the most agreeing points (inliers) wins.

cv_keypoint.title: Keypoint
cv_keypoint.definition: A locally distinctive image point, such as a corner or blob, that can be found reliably under changes in scale, rotation, and lighting.

cv_descriptor.title: Feature descriptor
cv_descriptor.definition: A numeric vector describing a keypoint's neighborhood so that the same point in two images can be matched by the distance between descriptors.

cv_sift_orb.title: SIFT and ORB
cv_sift_orb.definition: Keypoint detectors and descriptors. SIFT is robust to scale and rotation but heavy; ORB is a fast binary alternative for real time.

cv_matching_stitching.title: Matching and stitching
cv_matching_stitching.definition: Matching pairs up descriptors of two images; stitching assembles a panorama: a homography is estimated from the matches and the frames are merged into a common coordinate system.

nlp.title: NLP (Natural Language Processing)
nlp.definition: A field of machine learning and linguistics concerned with automatically processing and understanding human language. Tasks include text classification, NER, machine translation, generation, summarization, question answering, and more.

text_preprocessing.title: Text preprocessing
text_preprocessing.definition: Cleaning text of noise and vectorizing it: tokenization, stop-word removal, lemmatization/stemming, feature construction (TF-IDF, n-grams, embeddings). Done with classical pipelines or neural encoders.

corpus.title: Corpus
corpus.definition: A collection of documents (texts) used to train or evaluate NLP models. The size and quality of the corpus determine model quality.

tokenization.title: Tokenization
tokenization.definition: Splitting text into tokens (words, subwords, or characters). Can be word-level, subword (BPE, WordPiece), or character-level. The first step before vectorization or feeding text to a model.

stop_words.title: Stop words
stop_words.definition: Frequent words that carry little meaning (articles, prepositions, pronouns). Often removed in classical preprocessing; neural models may keep them.

lemmatization.title: Lemmatization
lemmatization.definition: Reducing word forms to their dictionary form (lemma). For example, "played" → "play", "children" → "child". Important for morphologically rich languages (such as Russian).

stemming.title: Stemming
stemming.definition: A simplified way to extract a word's stem without a full dictionary. Often produces a non-dictionary form. Used less than lemmatization in modern pipelines.

ngrams.title: N-grams
ngrams.definition: Sequences of n consecutive words (or characters). Bigrams, trigrams, etc. preserve local context; used in BoW, TF-IDF, and language models.

text_vectorization.title: Text vectorization
text_vectorization.definition: Converting text into numerical vectors for machine learning: one-hot, BoW, TF-IDF, embeddings (Word2Vec, BERT, etc.).

one_hot_nlp.title: One-hot representation
one_hot_nlp.definition: A vector the length of the vocabulary: 1 at the word's position, 0 elsewhere. It does not capture semantic similarity; historically the first way to vectorize words, rarely used today.

llm-as-a-judge.title: LLM as a Judge
llm-as-a-judge.definition: A method for evaluating LLM generation quality: a large model grades the output of a smaller model.

bow.title: Bag of Words (BoW)
bow.definition: Represents a document as a vector of word counts over a vocabulary. Word order is ignored. A simple method for classification and retrieval; it does not capture semantics or context.

distributional_semantics.title: Distributional semantics
distributional_semantics.definition: The idea that words appearing in similar contexts have similar meanings. The basis of count-based methods, PPMI, Word2Vec, and others.

tfidf.title: TF-IDF
tfidf.definition: The weight of a term in a document: TF (frequency in the document) $\times$ IDF (inverse document frequency). Highlights words important to a document relative to the whole collection. Widely used for retrieval and classification.

bm25.title: BM25
bm25.definition: A document-query relevance function: accounts for term frequencies with saturation and normalizes by document length. The standard in full-text search (Okapi BM25).

ppmi.title: PPMI (Positive Pointwise Mutual Information)
ppmi.definition: A measure of association between a word and a context: max(0, PMI). PMI shows how much more often a pair co-occurs than it would under independence. Used in word–context matrices and related to the idea behind Word2Vec.

lsa.title: LSA (Latent Semantic Analysis)
lsa.definition: A topic modeling method: SVD is applied to a term–document matrix (e.g., TF-IDF) to reduce dimensionality. Document and word vectors in the latent space reflect topics.

word2vec.title: Word2Vec
word2vec.definition: A method for learning dense word embeddings with a neural network. It is trained to predict the context from a word (Skip-Gram) or a word from its context (CBOW). Words with similar meanings get similar vectors.

glove.title: GloVe
glove.definition: Global Vectors for Word Representation: word embeddings trained on a co-occurrence matrix. Optimizes a weighted regression on log counts. Captures global corpus statistics.

fasttext.title: FastText
fasttext.definition: An extension of Word2Vec: a word is represented as the sum of its character n-gram vectors. This yields vectors for rare and unknown words (OOV).

bpe.title: BPE (Byte Pair Encoding)
bpe.definition: Subword tokenization: the most frequent pairs of characters/tokens are merged iteratively. Training produces a subword vocabulary; inference splits text using it. Used in GPT and RoBERTa.

wordpiece.title: WordPiece
wordpiece.definition: Subword tokenization: token pairs are merged by maximum likelihood score. Similar to BPE; used in BERT and ALBERT. The ## prefix marks a word continuation.

sentencepiece.title: SentencePiece
sentencepiece.definition: A subword tokenization framework: turns raw text (including text without spaces) into a token sequence and supports BPE and Unigram. Used in T5, ALBERT, and XLM-R.

bert.title: BERT
bert.definition: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers: an encoder-only model with bidirectional attention. Pretrained with MLM (token masking) and NSP. The basis for natural language understanding (NLU) tasks.

gpt.title: GPT
gpt.definition: Generative Pre-trained Transformer: a decoder-only model pretrained to predict the next token (language modeling). Uses unidirectional (causal) attention. The basis of generative LLMs.

seq2seq.title: Seq2Seq
seq2seq.definition: A sequence-to-sequence architecture: the encoder turns the input into a representation, and the decoder generates the output from it. Used in translation and summarization, often with attention.

language_model.title: Language model
language_model.definition: A model of the probability distribution over sequences of words/tokens. Usually predicts the next word from context. The basis of text generation and many pretrained models (GPT, BERT with MLM).

beam_search.title: Beam Search
beam_search.definition: A greedy-like search for generation: at each step, the k most probable continuations (beams) are kept. Balances greedy selection and exhaustive search; used in machine translation and generation.

sentence_transformers.title: Sentence Transformers
sentence_transformers.definition: Models for sentence embeddings: built on BERT/RoBERTa and others, trained so that semantically similar sentences get similar embeddings (triplet loss, contrastive learning). Used for semantic search and clustering.

ner.title: NER (Named Entity Recognition)
ner.definition: The task of finding named entities in text (people, organizations, dates, places, etc.) and assigning them a type. Solved with BIO/BIOES tags and models such as BiLSTM-CRF and BERT.

mqa.title: Multi-Query Attention (MQA)
mqa.definition: A variant of Multi-Head Attention: each head has its own Q, while K and V are shared across all heads. Reduces memory and speeds up inference; used in PaLM, StarCoder, and Falcon.

gqa.title: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)
gqa.definition: A compromise between MHA and MQA: heads are split into groups that share K and V, while each head keeps its own Q. Used in LLaMA 2 and Mistral.

rmsnorm.title: RMSNorm
rmsnorm.definition: Root Mean Square Normalization: normalizes by the root mean square over features (without subtracting the mean). Cheaper than LayerNorm and preserves the vector's direction; used in LLaMA, Falcon, and MPT.

alibi.title: ALiBi (Attention with Linear Biases)
alibi.definition: Positional encoding via a linear penalty in attention: a bias that depends on the distance between tokens is added to the logits. No positional embeddings are needed; it extrapolates to long contexts.

moe.title: Mixture of Experts (MoE)
moe.definition: A layer of several "experts" (subnetworks) where only some experts are active for each token (routing). Increases model capacity while bounding compute. Used in Mixtral and GShard.

nlp_context_window.title: Context window
nlp_context_window.definition: The maximum number of tokens a model sees at once, including the prompt and the response. Anything that does not fit is truncated; extending the window is expensive because attention is quadratic.

nlp_hallucination.title: Hallucinations
nlp_hallucination.definition: A confidently stated but incorrect model answer. Mitigated with RAG and source citations, fact-checking, and explicitly allowing the model to answer "I don't know."

nlp_perplexity.title: Perplexity
nlp_perplexity.definition: The exponent of a language model's average cross-entropy: how "surprised" the model is by the text. Lower means better prediction, but it correlates with answer quality only indirectly.

nlp_decoding_strategy.title: Decoding strategies (greedy, top-k, top-p)
nlp_decoding_strategy.definition: How the next token is chosen: greedy takes the maximum, top-k samples from the k best, and top-p (nucleus) samples from the smallest set with cumulative probability p. They affect diversity and coherence.

nlp_temperature.title: Sampling temperature
nlp_temperature.definition: A divisor applied to the logits before softmax: below one, the distribution gets sharper and answers more predictable; above one, more diverse and riskier. At 0, generation becomes deterministic.

nlp_autoregressive.title: Autoregressive generation
nlp_autoregressive.definition: Text is produced one token at a time: each next token is predicted from all previous ones and fed back as input. This explains the sequential nature and inference cost of LLMs.

nlp_rlhf.title: RLHF and DPO
nlp_rlhf.definition: Fine-tuning for human preferences: RLHF trains a reward model and optimizes the policy with PPO, while DPO skips the separate reward model and optimizes preferences directly.

nlp_special_tokens.title: Special tokens
nlp_special_tokens.definition: Reserved vocabulary tokens: [CLS] as an aggregate representation, [SEP] as a separator, [PAD] for length padding, [MASK] for MLM, [EOS] as the end of a sequence.

nlp_oov.title: OOV (out-of-vocabulary)
nlp_oov.definition: A word missing from the model's vocabulary. Subword tokenization solves the problem by splitting an unknown word into known pieces instead of replacing it with UNK.

llm_optimization.title: LLM Optimization
llm_optimization.definition: Speeding up inference and cutting the cost of large language models. Depends on the architecture (encoder/decoder-only), the task type (generation vs. classification), and the hardware (GPU, memory-bound). The goals are higher RPS and lower latency.

rps.title: RPS (requests per second)
rps.definition: The number of requests a service handles per second. Users want RPS as high as possible at acceptable latency.

latency.title: Latency
latency.definition: The time from a request to the service's response. A key inference quality metric alongside RPS; it should be minimized.

distillation.title: Knowledge Distillation
distillation.definition: Training a smaller student model to imitate the behavior of a large teacher model. Knowledge is transferred through a loss between teacher and student predictions, which lets you deploy compact models with fewer resources.

hard_label_distillation.title: Hard-label Distillation
hard_label_distillation.definition: Distillation in which the student is trained on input–output pairs generated by the teacher, as if they were supervised data. A simple approach: the teacher provides "hard" labels (specific tokens), and the student fits them.

soft_label_distillation.title: Soft-label Distillation
soft_label_distillation.definition: Distillation using the teacher's full probability distribution over the vocabulary (soft labels). The student minimizes the KL divergence between its distributions and the teacher's; this gives a richer training signal than hard-label distillation.

exposure_bias.title: Exposure Bias
exposure_bias.definition: A bias in distillation: the student learns from the teacher's outputs but generates on its own at inference. The mismatch between training and inference causes errors to accumulate; it is mitigated by on-policy distillation (training on the student's own generations).

minillm.title: MiniLLM
minillm.definition: On-policy LLM distillation: the student is trained on its own generations while minimizing the reverse KL divergence to the teacher. Gradients are estimated with the REINFORCE trick; training is stabilized with importance sampling and length-normalized rewards.

quantization.title: Quantization
quantization.definition: Converting values from a higher-precision representation (e.g., float32) to a more compact discrete one (int8, int4). In neural networks it shrinks the model and speeds it up at an acceptable loss of quality.

ptq.title: PTQ (Post-Training Quantization)
ptq.definition: Quantizing an already trained model without further training: scale and zero point are fitted on a calibration set. Cheap (little GPU time, ~1000 examples), but quality is usually lower than with QAT.

qat.title: QAT (Quantization-Aware Training)
qat.definition: Training or fine-tuning with quantization emulated in the layers. Produces models better suited to low precision; requires substantial compute (hundreds to thousands of GPU hours).

linear_quantization.title: Linear Quantization
linear_quantization.definition: The umbrella term for mapping a real-valued range to an integer range using a scale $s$ and, if needed, a zero point $z$. This family includes affine and symmetric quantization, the most common methods in neural networks.

affine_quantization.title: Affine (Asymmetric) Quantization
affine_quantization.definition: Linear quantization with a nonzero zero point: the range $[R_{min}, R_{max}]$ is mapped to a $k$-bit type via scale $s$ and zero point $z$. Formulas: $x_q = \lfloor x/s + z \rceil$, dequantization $x = s(x_q - z)$. Well suited to asymmetric distributions (e.g., ReLU outputs); more accurate than symmetric quantization but requires storing $z$.

symmetric_quantization.title: Symmetric Quantization
symmetric_quantization.definition: Linear quantization with zero point $z = 0$: a range symmetric around zero is mapped to integers (e.g., $[-127, 127]$ for int8). Scale $s = |R_{max}| / (2^{N-1}-1)$. Formulas: $x_q = \lfloor x/s \rceil$, $x = s \cdot x_q$. Simpler and faster than affine quantization, but worse on asymmetric data.

quantization_granularity.title: Quantization Granularity
quantization_granularity.definition: The level at which $s$ and $z$ (scale/zero point) are defined: for the whole model (per-tensor), per layer, per row/column, or per block. Coarser granularity means less metadata and more speed; finer granularity is more accurate and handles outliers better.

nf4.title: NF4 (NormalFloat4)
nf4.definition: A 4-bit type for quantizing neural network weights: its values are quantiles of the normal distribution in [-1, 1]. It exploits the fact that weights are often close to normally distributed; used in QLoRA.

w4a8.title: W4A8 / W4A4
w4a8.definition: A quantization scheme: $W$ is weights, $A$ is activations, the digit is the bit width. $W4A8$: 4-bit weights, 8-bit activations; $W4A4$: both in 4 bits (maximum savings, larger quality drop).

llm_int8.title: LLM.int8()
llm_int8.definition: A method for quantizing large LLMs to 8 bits: outliers in activations are handled separately (kept in 16 bits), and all other values go to 8 bits. Lets you quantize models with hundreds of billions of parameters with little quality loss, at the cost of more memory.

smoothquant.title: SmoothQuant
smoothquant.definition: Shifts quantization difficulty from activations (which have many outliers) to weights by multiplying activation columns and weight rows by a shared factor. The operations are "baked" into the weights offline; speeds up inference and reduces quality loss in 8-bit quantization.

gptq.title: GPTQ
gptq.definition: Column-wise weight quantization that accounts for the effect on the layer output (an approximation of Optimal Brain Quantization). Quantizes an LLM to $3$–$4$ bits in a few hours on a single A100; popular for inference (weights in $4$ bits, activations in $16$ bits).

awq.title: AWQ (Activation-Aware Weight Quantization)
awq.definition: Weight quantization that accounts for activations: calibration data is used to identify salient weights, which are kept unquantized or quantized more gently; the rest go to INT3/INT4. Reduces quality loss at the same compression ratio.

ggml_gguf.title: GGML / GGUF
ggml_gguf.definition: GGML is a C library and binary format for quantized models (originally Llama) that run on CPU. GGUF is its successor: a single extensible format for various LLMs. Quantization uses k-quants; models run via llama.cpp.

speculative_decoding.title: Speculative Decoding
speculative_decoding.definition: Speeding up LLM generation without quality loss: a small draft model proposes $K$ tokens ahead, and the large target model verifies them in a single pass, accepting or rejecting them. On average gives a $2\text{–}3\times$ generation speedup.

dynamic_batching.title: Dynamic Batching
dynamic_batching.definition: Combining several incoming requests into one batch for a joint pass through the model. The server waits for a short window, collects requests, and processes them in parallel; shorter ones are padded and masked. Improves GPU utilization under a stream of requests.

continuous_batching.title: Continuous Batching
continuous_batching.definition: Batching in which the batch changes on every iteration: finished requests free up slots for new ones. Eliminates GPU idle time caused by varying response lengths; gives a large throughput gain over static batching.

ragged_tensors.title: Ragged Tensors
ragged_tensors.definition: Tensors with variable length along a dimension (e.g., sequences of different lengths). They avoid padding in batches and wasted compute on padding tokens; used in continuous batching and long-context inference.

kv_cache.title: KV Cache
kv_cache.definition: Caching the keys and values ($K$, $V$) of already processed tokens in attention. During autoregressive generation it avoids recomputing $K$, $V$ for previous tokens at every step; greatly speeds up inference but grows linearly with context length and number of layers.

peft.title: PEFT (Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning)
peft.definition: Fine-tuning that updates only a fraction of the parameters: adapters (LoRA, QLoRA, VeRA, DoRA), prompts, and so on. Lets you tune large models with limited memory and store several adaptations on top of one base model.

lora.title: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)
lora.definition: A PEFT method: a low-rank update $\Delta W = B\cdot A$ is added to a linear layer ($A$ and $B$ are trained, the base is frozen). Forward pass: $y = W_0 x + (\alpha/r)\, B A x$. Far fewer trainable parameters and less VRAM; adapters can be merged into the base for inference with no overhead.

qlora.title: QLoRA (Quantized LoRA)
qlora.definition: Fine-tuning with a $4$-bit (NF4) base and trainable LoRA adapters in FP16. Forward pass: $y = \mathrm{dequant}(W_0^{\mathrm{NF4}})x + (\alpha/r) B A x$, i.e., on-the-fly weight dequantization plus the LoRA update. Double quantization reduces the memory for scales. Lets you tune large LLMs on a single GPU.

lora_plus.title: LoRA+
lora_plus.definition: A LoRA variant with different learning rates for matrices $A$ and $B$: $\eta_B = \lambda \eta_A$, $\lambda > 1$. Fixes the training imbalance in wide layers; improves quality and speeds up convergence at the same tuning cost.

vera.title: VeRA (Vector-based Random Matrix Adaptation)
vera.definition: PEFT: shared frozen random matrices $A$, $B$ across all layers; only scaling vectors (per row and column) are trained. Far fewer parameters than LoRA (up to $\sim 100\times$) at comparable quality; can be merged into the base.

dora.title: DoRA (Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation)
dora.definition: PEFT: the weight is decomposed into magnitude $m$ and direction $V$: $W_0 = m \frac{V}{\|V\|_c}$, updated as $W' = m \frac{V + \Delta V}{\|V + \Delta V\|_c}$, where $\Delta V = B A$ (LoRA). The direction is updated with a low-rank increment, the magnitude with a separate trainable vector. Approximates full fine-tuning's expressiveness better than plain LoRA.

flash_attention.title: FlashAttention
flash_attention.definition: An optimization of self-attention computation: tiling over blocks of $Q$, $K$, $V$ in fast memory (SRAM) and minimizing transfers to and from HBM. Preserves the mathematical result (or nearly so in FP16), sharply reduces memory, and speeds up transformer training and inference.

rag.title: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
rag.definition: An approach to text generation: retrieve relevant passages from a knowledge base, augment the query context with them, and generate the answer with an LLM. Knowledge lives outside the model, which reduces hallucinations and lets data be updated without retraining.

rag_chunk.title: Chunk
rag_chunk.definition: A text fragment that documents are split into for RAG. Chunks are indexed in a vector database and passed to the LLM as context. Chunking quality affects retrieval and answer quality.

rag_chunking.title: Chunking
rag_chunking.definition: Splitting documents into small fragments (chunks) for indexing and retrieval in RAG. Strategies: by characters/tokens, by separators, by Markdown structure, semantic chunking, proposition chunking. Affects context quality, index size, and latency.

rag_retrieve.title: Retrieve
rag_retrieve.definition: The RAG stage that searches the knowledge base for text passages relevant to the user's query, usually via vector search over embeddings (dense/sparse) or hybrid search. Retrieval quality directly determines answer quality.

rag_vector_db.title: Vector Database
rag_vector_db.definition: A store of vector representations (embeddings) of texts for fast similarity search. In RAG it is used to find relevant chunks and implements ANN (approximate nearest neighbor) search. Examples: FAISS, Qdrant, ChromaDB, Milvus, Pinecone.

rag_embedding.title: Embedding (in RAG)
rag_embedding.definition: A vector representation of a text (or chunk) in a high-dimensional space; semantically similar texts have nearby vectors. In RAG an embedder encodes queries and documents for vector search. Types: dense, sparse, long-context, code embeddings.

rag_ann.title: ANN (Approximate Nearest Neighbor)
rag_ann.definition: Approximate nearest neighbor search in a vector space. Scales search to millions of vectors with acceptable latency; used in vector databases for RAG retrieval.

rag_naive_advanced_modular.title: Naive / Advanced / Modular RAG
rag_naive_advanced_modular.definition: RAG paradigms: Naive RAG is the indexing → retrieval → generation chain; Advanced RAG adds pre- and post-retrieval optimizations; Modular RAG is a flexible architecture with swappable modules and iterative, adaptive retrieval.

rag_hybrid_search.title: Hybrid Search
rag_hybrid_search.definition: Combining semantic vector search (dense) with lexical search (BM25, sparse) to account for both query meaning and exact term matches. Results are merged via a weighted sum or RRF (Reciprocal Rank Fusion); improves recall and robustness.

rag_rrf.title: RRF (Reciprocal Rank Fusion)
rag_rrf.definition: A way to merge results from several rankers (e.g., dense and sparse): $\mathrm{score}(d) = \sum_{r \in R} \frac{1}{k + \mathrm{rank}_r(d)}$, where $k$ is a smoothing constant and $\mathrm{rank}_r(d)$ is the rank of document $d$ in ranker $r$'s results. Needs no score calibration; common in hybrid search for RAG.

rag_reranker.title: Reranker
rag_reranker.definition: A model or rule that reorders retrieval candidates by relevance to the query. In RAG it is the second stage after fast retrieval: a cross-encoder or LLM-based judge processes the top-$k$ chunks and selects the best for the LLM context. Increases precision and reduces context noise.

rag_cross_encoder.title: Cross-Encoder (in RAG)
rag_cross_encoder.definition: A model that takes a (query, document/chunk) pair and outputs a relevance score. Used as a reranker: slower than ANN search but more accurate thanks to jointly encoding the query and the chunk.

rag_metrics.title: RAG Metrics
rag_metrics.definition: Stage-by-stage quality evaluation: retrieval (Recall@$k$, Precision@$k$, MAP), generation (ROUGE, BERTScore, BLEU), embeddings (MTEB, cosine similarity), fact consistency (FactCC, QAGS), end to end (LLM-as-judge, factoid scoring).

rag_mteb.title: MTEB
rag_mteb.definition: A library and benchmark for evaluating embedding quality across many tasks (retrieval, clustering, classification, etc.) and datasets. Used to compare embedders for RAG and search.

rag_dense_sparse.title: Dense / Sparse Embeddings
rag_dense_sparse.definition: Dense: compact vectors, the main tool for semantic search in RAG. Sparse: sparse representations close to bag-of-words that handle domain terminology and exact matches well. Hybrid search often combines both.

rag_frameworks.title: RAG Frameworks
rag_frameworks.definition: Libraries for building RAG systems: document loading, chunking, indexing, retrieval, reranking, LLM integration. Examples: LangChain (chains, agents), LlamaIndex (ingestion, retrieval), Haystack (production pipelines). They speed up prototyping; quality depends on the data and stage tuning.

rag_production.title: Production RAG
rag_production.definition: Engineering aspects of running RAG: ingestion pipeline, online retrieval with hybrid search and a reranker, monitoring (latency, quality, cost), index versioning, handling no-hit queries and hallucinations, logging candidates, and citing sources.

rag_no_hit.title: No-hit Query
rag_no_hit.definition: A query for which retrieval found no relevant chunks. In production, leaving it unhandled leads to hallucinations; it needs a fallback ("nothing found", a prompt to refine the query) and no-hit rate monitoring.

rag_topk_metrics.title: Recall@k and Precision@k
rag_topk_metrics.definition: Retrieval metrics: Recall@k is the share of relevant documents that made it into the top k; Precision@k is the share of relevant documents among the k returned. Computed before generation, separately from answer quality.

llm_agent.title: LLM Agent
llm_agent.definition: An architecture in which an LLM does more than generate text: it produces structured outputs, calls external functions (tools, APIs, databases), and solves tasks step by step, combining reasoning and actions. Key components: Structured Outputs, tool/function calling, ReAct, frameworks (LangChain, LangGraph).

structured_output.title: Structured Output (SO)
structured_output.definition: LLM responses in a strictly defined structure (e.g., JSON matching a schema) that are easy to process programmatically. A bridge between the conversational nature of LLMs and the requirements of code. Approaches: prompt instructions, few-shot, built-in JSON/Schema mode, function calling, constrained decoding.

tool_calling.title: Tool Calling / Function Calling
tool_calling.definition: A mechanism in which the LLM returns a structured function call (JSON with a name and arguments) instead of text. The host system executes the call and returns the result to the model. Turns the LLM into "an agent that can act". Supported by OpenAI, Anthropic, vLLM, LangChain.

react.title: ReAct (Reason + Act)
react.definition: A prompting pattern in which the model alternates thoughts (Thought) and actions (Action). The agent reasons, calls a tool, receives an Observation, thinks again, and so on. Reduces hallucinations and adds transparency and flexibility; costs more tokens than one-shot function calling.

chain_of_thought.title: Chain-of-Thought (CoT)
chain_of_thought.definition: A prompting technique in which the model explicitly generates a chain of intermediate reasoning before the final answer, forcing the LLM to solve step by step. Sharply improves accuracy on reasoning tasks (math, logic, QA). Some APIs use "hidden" CoT.

schema_guided_reasoning.title: Schema-Guided Reasoning (SGR)
schema_guided_reasoning.definition: An approach in which the model reasons and outputs results strictly according to a given schema (JSON Schema, Pydantic, OpenAPI). A hybrid of CoT and Structured Output; reduces hallucinations and makes reasoning machine-readable. Useful in the enterprise (lending, medicine, legal analysis).

multiagent_systems.title: Multi-Agent Systems
multiagent_systems.definition: Architectures in which several LLM agents work together, each with its own role, memory, and tools (Planner, Researcher, Coder, Critic, etc.). Interaction modes: sequential, parallel (swarm), consensus, hierarchy (planner $\to$ workers). Examples: CrewAI, LangGraph, Deep Research.

agent_swarm.title: Agent Swarm
agent_swarm.definition: A large number of simple agents that explore the solution space in parallel and collectively reach a better answer (voting, selection). Unlike a hierarchy (planner $\to$ workers), the agents are independent. Effective for search and brainstorming, poorly suited to strict business processes.

human_in_the_loop.title: Human-in-the-Loop
human_in_the_loop.definition: An approach in which a person can intervene in the agent's work: approve, edit, or stop steps. Improves control and safety; often mandatory for sensitive actions (payments, publishing).

mcp.title: MCP (Model Context Protocol)
mcp.definition: An open protocol (Anthropic, 2024) that standardizes interaction between an LLM client and external tools/resources. It defines discovery (list_tools), invocation (call_tool), resource access, and transport. Tools live in an MCP server, and the agent connects as a client; it reduces "information silos" and simplifies scaling.

orchestrator.title: Orchestrator
orchestrator.definition: The component of an agent system that controls the order of agent calls, transitions between steps, state, and stops/retries. It decomposes the task, hands pieces to subagents, and merges the results. Without an orchestrator the logic is baked into one agent, which is hard to debug and extend with new agents.

subagent.title: Subagent
subagent.definition: A specialized agent with a distinct role (researcher, coder, critic) managed by the orchestrator. It performs its task, returns the result to the orchestrator, and has access to a set of tools.

browser_use.title: Browser-use
