browser_use.definition: An open-source framework for LLM agents that drive a real browser (Chromium/Playwright): open sites, click, type text, run multi-step web scenarios. What sets it apart is how interactive elements are identified and passed to the LLM, which improves action selection. Use cases: automation without an API, E2E tests.

deep_research.title: Deep Research
deep_research.definition: An approach to automated research: the agent plans queries, runs web search and extraction, validates sources, aggregates facts, and builds reports. Goes beyond RAG or a single search; typically uses parallel search (Tavily, Firecrawl, SerpAPI, etc.) and structured output with citations.

agent_benchmarks.title: Agent Benchmarks
agent_benchmarks.definition: Task sets and environments for evaluating LLMs as agents: multi-step interaction, decision-making, tool use, and reaching goals in an open environment. Unlike classic NLP benchmarks, they test agentic behavior, not just text generation.

context_engineering.title: Context Engineering
context_engineering.definition: The practice of designing and selecting the optimal set of tokens passed to the LLM at each step: not just phrasing the request, but the whole context configuration (system prompt, tools, history, RAG, memory). Accounts for the limited context and the context rot effect; in agents the prompt is only part of the context.

local_memory.title: Agent Local Memory
local_memory.definition: An agent's ability to store and retrieve information about past steps within a session: what was done, what was found, which decisions were made. The agent's working state between steps; not "knowledge in general" but context for the next actions.

agent_langchain.title: LangChain and LangGraph
agent_langchain.definition: Agent frameworks: LangChain provides wrappers for LLMs, tools, and memory; LangGraph describes an agent as a state graph with explicit transitions and breakpoints.

ts_time_series.title: Time Series
ts_time_series.definition: A sequence of observations $y_1,\ldots,y_T$ ordered in time. Order matters: today's value depends on the past; randomly shuffling before training leaks the future.

ts_forecast_horizon.title: Forecast Horizon
ts_forecast_horizon.definition: The number of future steps to predict: one-step ($\hat y_{t+1}$) or multi-step ($\hat y_{t+1},\ldots,\hat y_{t+h}$). A long horizon is usually harder and less stable.

ts_trend.title: Trend
ts_trend.definition: The long-term direction of change in the series level (growth, decline, slow drift). Often denoted $T_t$ in decomposition.

ts_seasonality.title: Seasonality
ts_seasonality.definition: A recurring pattern with a known period (day, week, year): $S_t$. It differs from a cycle by its fixed period and from noise by its regularity.

ts_stationarity.title: Stationarity
ts_stationarity.definition: Weak stationarity: constant mean and variance, and the covariance of $y_t$ and $y_{t-k}$ depends only on the lag $k$. Many classical models (ARMA) are convenient to build on a stationary series; trend and seasonality break stationarity.

ts_heteroscedasticity.title: Heteroscedasticity
ts_heteroscedasticity.definition: The variance of the series or errors changes over time or with the level of the series. Stabilized with a logarithm, Box–Cox, or other transformations.

ts_box_cox.title: Box–Cox Transformation
ts_box_cox.definition: A family of power transformations of a positive series that stabilize variance; as $\lambda\to 0$ it becomes the logarithm.

ts_differencing.title: Differencing
ts_differencing.definition: The first difference $\Delta y_t=y_t-y_{t-1}$ removes a linear trend; the seasonal difference $\Delta_s y_t=y_t-y_{t-s}$ works with period $s$. The order $d$ in ARIMA is the number of ordinary differences.

ts_acf.title: ACF
ts_acf.definition: Autocorrelation function: the correlation of $y_t$ with $y_{t-k}$ across lags $k$. Helps reveal seasonality and dependence on the past.

ts_pacf.title: PACF
ts_pacf.definition: Partial autocorrelation: the contribution of lag $k$ after accounting for lags $1,\ldots,k-1$. Together with the ACF it suggests the AR/MA orders.

ts_arima_family.title: AR, MA, ARMA, ARIMA, SARIMA
ts_arima_family.definition: AR($p$): linear dependence on past values; MA($q$): on past errors; ARMA combines them; ARIMA adds integration (differencing) of order $d$; SARIMA adds seasonal components; SARIMAX adds exogenous features.

ts_exponential_smoothing.title: Exponential Smoothing
ts_exponential_smoothing.definition: The smoothed level as an exponentially weighted sum of past observations; generalizations (Holt, Holt–Winters) add trend and seasonality.

ts_backtesting.title: Backtesting / Walk-Forward
ts_backtesting.definition: Evaluating a model on several consecutive time slices: train on the past, validate on the near future, then expand the window. Less optimistic than a single random split.

ts_temporal_split.title: Temporal Split
ts_temporal_split.definition: Splitting train/test by time: the model is trained only on the past and evaluated on the future, as in production.

ts_future_leakage.title: Future Leakage
ts_future_leakage.definition: Using information during training or in features that is not yet available at real forecast time (e.g., future series values in a rolling feature). Inflates the metrics.

ts_mape.title: MAPE / sMAPE
ts_mape.definition: Mean Absolute Percentage Error and its symmetric variant, measuring relative forecast error. Sensitive to small denominators and zeros in $y_t$.

ts_adf_kpss.title: ADF and KPSS
ts_adf_kpss.definition: Statistical tests for a unit root / stationarity; interpret them together with plots and domain knowledge, not as the sole source of truth.

rec_recommender_system.title: Recommender System
rec_recommender_system.definition: A model or pipeline that selects catalog items for a user based on history and context. Typically: users $U$, items $I$, interactions with signal $y_{ui}$, time, and context.

rec_collaborative_filtering.title: Collaborative Filtering
rec_collaborative_filtering.definition: Recommendations based on interaction patterns: similar users/items (user-user / item-item), without necessarily relying on item content.

rec_content_based.title: Content-based Recommendations
rec_content_based.definition: Matching based on item features and the user profile (text, categories, attributes), without relying on similar people.

rec_implicit_feedback.title: Implicit / Explicit Feedback
rec_implicit_feedback.definition: Explicit: ratings, likes. Implicit: clicks, views, purchases, dwell time; larger in scale but noisier (a missing event ≠ a negative).

rec_cold_start.title: Cold Start
rec_cold_start.definition: A new user or item with no history, which makes it hard to estimate preferences or quality. Addressed with popular items, content, rules, or falling back to search.

rec_long_tail.title: Long-tail Problem
rec_long_tail.definition: Most impressions go to the popular head of the catalog, while niche items in the long tail get almost no data or exposure.

rec_exposure_bias.title: Exposure / Popularity Bias
rec_exposure_bias.definition: Distortion of training data because users saw only part of the catalog; popular items get more clicks not only because of preference.

rec_feedback_loop.title: Feedback Loop
rec_feedback_loop.definition: The system reinforces its past decisions: whatever was shown gathers more signal. Exploration, randomization, and bias correction are needed.

rec_matrix_factorization.title: Matrix Factorization
rec_matrix_factorization.definition: A low-rank approximation of the user–item matrix, $\hat r_{ui}\approx \mathbf p_u^\top\mathbf q_i$; the basis of latent factor models and many neural scoring models.

rec_funksvd.title: FunkSVD / ALS / PMF
rec_funksvd.definition: FunkSVD: SGD with $\ell_2$ on observed $(u,i)$. ALS: alternating least squares over users and items. PMF: a probabilistic formulation whose MAP estimate is equivalent to a regularized squared loss.

rec_wrmf.title: WRMF
rec_wrmf.definition: Weighted Regularized Matrix Factorization for implicit feedback: weights $c_{ui}$ reflect confidence in positive events; zeros are not treated as hard negatives.

rec_bpr.title: BPR Loss
rec_bpr.definition: Bayesian Personalized Ranking: pairwise ranking in which a positive item should score higher than a sampled negative; optimized via $\log\sigma(\hat y_{ui}-\hat y_{uj})$.

rec_two_stage.title: Retrieval and Ranking
rec_two_stage.definition: A two-stage scheme: fast candidate generation (retrieval) from a large catalog, then precise ranking of a short list. Retrieval is responsible for recall.

rec_two_tower.title: Two-Tower
rec_two_tower.definition: Separate user and item encoders; the score is a dot product or cosine; item vectors are precomputed and the user vector is computed online, which suits ANN search over the catalog.

rec_ann.title: ANN (Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search)
rec_ann.definition: Approximate nearest neighbor search over embeddings: FAISS, HNSW, IVF, PQ, ScaNN; a speed/quality trade-off for large catalogs.

rec_ndcg.title: NDCG
rec_ndcg.definition: Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain: a ranking quality metric with a position discount; supports graded relevance.

rec_mrr.title: MRR
rec_mrr.definition: Mean Reciprocal Rank: the average $1/rank$ of the first relevant document; suitable when the first correct answer is what matters.

rec_map_ranking.title: MAP (Ranking)
rec_map_ranking.definition: Mean Average Precision averages AP over queries/users; accounts for the order of multiple relevant items.

rec_dwell_time.title: Dwell Time
rec_dwell_time.definition: Time spent viewing or interacting with an item, used as an interest signal in implicit feedback.

rec_sequential.title: Sequential Recommendations
rec_sequential.definition: Models over action sequences (RNN, Transformer, SASRec): predict the next item from the history of clicks or purchases.

rec_bandit.title: Bandits and Exploration
rec_bandit.definition: Multi-armed bandits and exploration–exploitation policies (ε-greedy, Thompson sampling, UCB) balance showing new items against exploiting known good ones.

rec_hybrid_system.title: Hybrid Recommender
rec_hybrid_system.definition: A combination of CF, content, rules, graphs, and popularity for robustness and cold start.

rec_reranking.title: Re-ranking
rec_reranking.definition: The second stage of recommendations and search: a heavy model reorders a few hundred candidates selected by fast retrieval. Diversity and business rules are also applied here.

py_mutability.title: Mutable and Immutable Types
py_mutability.definition: A mutable object can be changed in place (list, dict, set); an immutable one cannot (int, str, tuple, frozenset). "Modifying" an immutable object creates a new one.

py_decorator.title: Decorator
py_decorator.definition: A function that takes another function and returns a wrapper around it, adding behavior (logging, caching, timing) without changing the original code. Applied with the @name syntax.

py_iterator.title: Iterator
py_iterator.definition: An object with __iter__ and __next__ that yields items one at a time and raises StopIteration at the end. It keeps its current position, so it can be traversed only once.

py_iterable.title: Iterable
py_iterable.definition: An object you can loop over with for: it can return an iterator via __iter__. Lists, strings, dicts, and files are iterable; an iterator is iterable too.

py_generator.title: Generator Function (yield)
py_generator.definition: A function with yield: it produces values lazily, one at a time, keeping its state between calls. It does not hold the whole sequence in memory, which suits large data and streams.

py_context_manager.title: Context Manager (with)
py_context_manager.definition: An object with __enter__ and __exit__ that guarantees a resource (file, connection, lock) is released when the with block exits, including on an exception.

py_comprehension.title: Comprehension
py_comprehension.definition: A compact way to build a list, dict, or set from an iterable: [f(x) for x in xs if cond]. Reads better than a loop and is usually faster than append in a loop.

py_closure.title: Closure
py_closure.definition: A nested function that remembers variables from its enclosing scope and still sees them after the outer function has returned. The basis of decorators and function factories.

py_scope_legb.title: Scope (LEGB)
py_scope_legb.definition: The name lookup order: Local → Enclosing → Global → Built-in. The global and nonlocal keywords allow assigning to variables from outer scopes.

py_identity_equality.title: Identity vs. Equality (is and ==)
py_identity_equality.definition: == compares values (via __eq__); is checks whether two references point to the same object in memory (same id). By convention, None, True, and False are compared with is.

py_hashable.title: Hashability (__hash__)
py_hashable.definition: An object is hashable if it has a hash that never changes and a consistent __eq__. Only hashable objects can be dict keys and set elements; lists and dicts are not.

py_dunder.title: Dunder Method (Magic Method)
py_dunder.definition: A method with double underscores (__init__, __len__, __eq__, __repr__) that Python calls implicitly: on object creation, len(), comparison, printing.

py_args_kwargs.title: *args and **kwargs
py_args_kwargs.definition: Syntax for accepting any number of arguments: *args collects positional ones into a tuple, **kwargs collects keyword ones into a dict. At call time, the same stars unpack arguments.

py_mutable_default.title: Mutable Default Argument
py_mutable_default.definition: A classic trap: a default value is evaluated once, when the function is defined, so a shared list or dict accumulates data across calls. Use None and create the object inside.

py_inheritance.title: Inheritance
py_inheritance.definition: An OOP mechanism: a subclass gets the parent's attributes and methods and can override them. With multiple inheritance, the method lookup order is defined by the MRO.

py_polymorphism.title: Polymorphism
py_polymorphism.definition: The ability to work with objects of different classes through a common interface: the same call behaves differently depending on the object's type.

py_encapsulation.title: Encapsulation
py_encapsulation.definition: Hiding an object's internal state behind a public interface. In Python it is a convention: _name is "internal", __name triggers name mangling; there is no strict private.

py_property.title: @property (Getters and Setters)
py_property.definition: A decorator that turns a method into a computed attribute: it is accessed like a field, but code runs underneath. Lets you add validation without changing the class's external interface.

py_classmethod.title: @classmethod and @staticmethod
py_classmethod.definition: A classmethod receives the class (cls) as its first argument and usually serves as an alternative constructor; a staticmethod receives neither self nor cls and is just a function in the class namespace.

py_type_hints.title: Type Hints
py_type_hints.definition: Optional type annotations (x: int, -> str, Optional, Union). The interpreter does not check them (mypy, pyright, or ty do), but IDEs, linters, and Pydantic read them.

py_fstring.title: f-string
py_fstring.definition: String formatting with expressions embedded directly in the literal: f"{x:.2f}". Faster than % and .format(), supports format specifiers and the debug syntax f"{x=}".

py_exception.title: Exception
py_exception.definition: An error object that interrupts normal execution. Caught with try/except, raised with raise; the finally block always runs, else runs only if no error occurred.

py_lambda.title: Lambda Function
py_lambda.definition: An anonymous single-expression function: lambda x: x * 2. Used as a short callback in sorted, map, filter; for anything more complex, a regular def is preferred.

py_pep8.title: PEP 8
py_pep8.definition: The Python style guide: indentation, line length, naming, imports. Automatically checked and applied by linters and formatters (ruff, black).

py_regex.title: Regular Expression
py_regex.definition: A language for describing text patterns; in Python, the re module. Lets you search, validate, and replace substrings by pattern, but becomes hard to read for complex grammars.

pya_gil.title: GIL (Global Interpreter Lock)
pya_gil.definition: CPython's global interpreter lock: only one thread in a process executes bytecode at a time. That is why threads speed up I/O-bound work but not CPU-bound work, which needs processes.

pya_cpython.title: CPython
pya_cpython.definition: The reference implementation of Python, written in C, which most people have installed. It is the one with the GIL, reference counting, and bytecode in __pycache__; alternatives include PyPy, Jython, and GraalPy.

pya_coroutine.title: Coroutine
pya_coroutine.definition: A function declared with async def: its execution can be suspended at await and resumed later. It does not run on its own; the event loop executes it.

pya_event_loop.title: Event loop
pya_event_loop.definition: The asyncio scheduler: it keeps a queue of tasks and switches between coroutines at await points while they wait on I/O. Everything runs in a single thread, without preemption.

pya_asyncio.title: asyncio (async/await)
pya_asyncio.definition: The standard library for cooperative multitasking: async def declares a coroutine, and await yields control to the event loop. It pays off for I/O-bound tasks, not for computation.

pya_threading.title: Multithreading (threading)
pya_threading.definition: Multiple threads inside one process sharing memory. Because of the GIL, it only speeds up waiting (network, disk); shared memory requires synchronization with a Lock.

pya_multiprocessing.title: Multiprocessing
pya_multiprocessing.definition: Parallel execution in separate processes, each with its own memory and its own GIL: true parallelism for CPU-bound tasks. The cost is startup overhead and pickle serialization of data.

pya_cpu_io_bound.title: CPU-bound and I/O-bound
pya_cpu_io_bound.definition: A CPU-bound task is limited by computation (training, parsing); an I/O-bound task by waiting on the network or disk. This determines the choice: processes for the former, threads or asyncio for the latter.

pya_race_condition.title: Race condition
pya_race_condition.definition: A bug where the result depends on the order in which threads run: two threads read and write a shared variable interleaved. Fixed with locks or immutable data.

pya_lock.title: Lock (mutex)
pya_lock.definition: A synchronization primitive: only one thread can hold the lock at a time. It protects a critical section, but acquiring locks in a careless order leads to a deadlock.

pya_gc.title: Garbage collector (GC)
pya_gc.definition: In CPython, reference counting is the foundation; an additional generational collector traverses objects and breaks reference cycles that the counter cannot free on its own.

pya_refcount.title: Reference counting
pya_refcount.definition: Each object stores the number of references to it; when it drops to zero, memory is freed immediately. Reference cycles never reach zero, so the generational collector cleans them up.

pya_weakref.title: Weak reference (weakref)
pya_weakref.definition: A reference that does not increase the reference count and does not prevent the object from being deleted. Used for caches and back-references so objects are not kept in memory longer than needed.

pya_copy_deepcopy.title: Shallow and deep copy
pya_copy_deepcopy.definition: copy() creates a new container, but nested objects remain shared; deepcopy() recursively copies the whole structure. This explains "unexpected" changes through nested lists.

pya_dataclass.title: @dataclass
pya_dataclass.definition: A decorator that generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ from field annotations. frozen=True makes the object immutable and hashable; unlike Pydantic, there is no type validation.

pya_namedtuple.title: namedtuple / NamedTuple
pya_namedtuple.definition: An immutable tuple with named fields: accessible by both index and name. Lighter than a class in memory and supports unpacking, but its fields cannot be changed.

pya_pydantic.title: Pydantic BaseModel
pya_pydantic.definition: A data model with validation and type coercion based on annotations: parses JSON, returns clear errors, and handles serialization. The basis of schemas in FastAPI and LLM structured output.

pya_abc.title: Abstract base class (ABC)
pya_abc.definition: A class that cannot be instantiated: it defines an interface via @abstractmethod, and subclasses must provide the implementation. It enforces the contract in code rather than by convention.

pya_duck_typing.title: Duck typing
pya_duck_typing.definition: An approach where what matters is not an object's type but whether it has the needed methods: if an object behaves like a file, it can be used as a file. Hence the preference for try/except over isinstance.

pya_metaclass.title: Metaclass
pya_metaclass.definition: A class that creates classes: it intercepts their construction and can modify attributes and methods. The mechanism behind ORMs, Pydantic, and ABC; rarely needed in application code.

pya_bytecode.title: Bytecode and __pycache__
pya_bytecode.definition: Source code is compiled to bytecode and cached in __pycache__/*.pyc so it is not recompiled. Cache freshness is checked by modification time or file hash.

pya_venv.title: Virtual environment
pya_venv.definition: An isolated set of project dependencies (.venv, uv, conda) so library versions do not conflict between projects and are reproducible for teammates and in CI.

pya_linter.title: Linter and formatter
pya_linter.definition: A linter (ruff, flake8) finds bugs and style violations without running the code; a formatter (black, ruff format) makes formatting uniform. Usually hooked into pre-commit and CI.

pya_profiling.title: Profiling
pya_profiling.definition: Measuring where time or memory goes: cProfile and py-spy per function, memory_profiler for memory, and flame graphs to visualize the stack. Optimize only what the profile shows.

pya_jit_numba.title: JIT compilation (numba)
pya_jit_numba.definition: Compiling hot functions to machine code at runtime. numba with @njit speeds up numeric loops many times over, but supports only a subset of Python and its types.

pya_vectorization.title: Vectorization (NumPy)
pya_vectorization.definition: Replacing element-by-element loops with operations on whole arrays: the computation moves into compiled C code and runs tens of times faster than Python lists.

pya_broadcasting.title: Broadcasting
pya_broadcasting.definition: A NumPy and PyTorch rule: arrays of different shapes are automatically stretched to a compatible shape without copying data. Saves memory but hides shape bugs.

pya_pickle.title: pickle (serialization)
pya_pickle.definition: Python's built-in format for serializing objects to bytes. Used by multiprocessing and caches, but unsafe: loading an untrusted pickle is equivalent to executing someone else's code.

alg_hash_table.title: Hash Table
alg_hash_table.definition: A structure where a hash function maps a key to a bucket index: O(1) access on average. dict and set are built on it; under heavy collisions, complexity degrades to O(n).

alg_complexity.title: Asymptotic Complexity (Big O)
alg_complexity.definition: An estimate of how time or memory grows with input size: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²). Constants are dropped; only the order of growth matters.

alg_amortized.title: Amortized Complexity
alg_amortized.definition: The average cost per operation over a long sequence. For example, a list append occasionally reallocates the array in O(n), but on average each operation costs O(1).

alg_space_complexity.title: Space Complexity (In-Place)
alg_space_complexity.definition: How much extra memory an algorithm needs beyond its input. An algorithm with O(1) extra memory is in-place: it works directly in the original array.

alg_collision.title: Hash Collision
alg_collision.definition: When different keys map to the same bucket index. Resolved by chaining or open addressing; mass collisions turn O(1) into O(n).

alg_hash_function.title: Hash Function
alg_hash_function.definition: A function mapping an object to a fixed-size integer. Equal objects must get equal hashes; the converse does not hold, and that is exactly a collision.

alg_two_pointers.title: Two Pointers
alg_two_pointers.definition: Traversing a sorted sequence with two indices moving toward each other or one after the other. Replaces an O(n²) nested loop with a single O(n) pass.

alg_sliding_window.title: Sliding Window
alg_sliding_window.definition: Scanning a sequence with a fixed- or variable-length window, updating the aggregate at the edges instead of recomputing from scratch. Gives O(n) instead of O(n·k).

alg_stack.title: Stack (LIFO)
alg_stack.definition: A last-in, first-out structure: push and pop in O(1) at one end. In Python, list plays the role of a stack; the function call stack works the same way.

alg_queue.title: Queue (FIFO, deque)
alg_queue.definition: A first-in, first-out structure. In Python, use collections.deque: insertion and removal at both ends in O(1), unlike list.pop(0) at O(n).

alg_dfs.title: DFS (Depth-First Search)
alg_dfs.definition: Traversing a graph or tree as deep as possible before backtracking. Implemented with recursion or an explicit stack; O(depth) memory; suited to finding components and topological sorting.

alg_bfs.title: BFS (Breadth-First Search)
alg_bfs.definition: Level-by-level traversal using a queue. Finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph; memory is O(level width), which on dense graphs exceeds that of DFS.

alg_dp.title: Dynamic Programming
alg_dp.definition: Breaking a problem into overlapping subproblems and storing their solutions. Implemented bottom-up with a table or top-down with memoized recursion.

alg_memoization.title: Memoization
alg_memoization.definition: Caching a function's results by its arguments to avoid computing the same thing twice. In Python, functools.lru_cache or cache on top of a pure function.

alg_recursion.title: Recursion
alg_recursion.definition: A function that calls itself on a smaller problem, with a base case to stop. Depth is limited by the call stack, so deep recursion is rewritten as a loop.

alg_binary_search.title: Binary Search
alg_binary_search.definition: Searching a sorted array by halving in O(log n). In Python, the bisect module; also applied to "binary search on the answer" over a monotonic predicate.

alg_timsort.title: Timsort (Stable Sort)
alg_timsort.definition: A hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort used by sorted() and list.sort(): O(n log n) worst case, O(n) on nearly sorted data, stable for equal keys.

alg_flops.title: FLOPS and FLOPs
alg_flops.definition: FLOPS measures hardware speed (floating-point operations per second); FLOPs measures a model's amount of computation. The former describes a GPU, the latter the cost of running a network.

lnx_pipe.title: Pipe (|)
lnx_pipe.definition: Passes the stdout of one command to the stdin of the next: ps aux | grep python. Data flows as a stream without intermediate files, which is handy for large logs.

lnx_redirect.title: Output redirection (stdout, stderr)
lnx_redirect.definition: Streams: stdout (1) is regular output, stderr (2) is errors. > writes to a file, >> appends, and 2>&1 merges errors into the same stream as the output.

lnx_ssh.title: SSH and SSH keys
lnx_ssh.definition: A protocol for secure access to a remote machine. Instead of a password, a key pair is used: the private key stays local, and the public key goes into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server.

lnx_tmux.title: tmux
lnx_tmux.definition: A terminal multiplexer: sessions live on the server and survive a dropped SSH connection. A session contains windows and panes; detach to disconnect, tmux attach to return.

lnx_background_job.title: Background process (nohup, &)
lnx_background_job.definition: Running a task that survives closing the terminal: & sends it to the background, nohup detaches it from the session, and disown removes it from the shell's job list. Output is usually written to a log file.

lnx_oom.title: OOM killer
lnx_oom.definition: A kernel mechanism: when RAM runs out, it kills the most memory-hungry process. In the logs, it looks like training suddenly dying without a traceback.

lnx_pid.title: PID (process ID)
lnx_pid.definition: A number the kernel assigns to a process at startup. It is used to find the process in ps and htop and to send it signals via kill.

lnx_signals.title: Signals (SIGTERM, SIGKILL)
lnx_signals.definition: kill sends a signal to a process: SIGTERM (15) asks it to exit gracefully and can be caught; SIGKILL (9) kills it instantly with no chance to save state.

lnx_permissions.title: File permissions (chmod, rwx)
lnx_permissions.definition: Three permission groups (owner, group, others) with bits r (4), w (2), x (1). Hence the octal notation chmod 755: full access for the owner, read and execute for everyone else.

lnx_chown.title: Owner and group (chown)
lnx_chown.definition: Every file has an owning user and a group; chown changes them. A common cause of permission errors in Docker is files created by root inside a container.

lnx_symlink.title: Symbolic link (symlink)
lnx_symlink.definition: A file that points to another path, created with ln -s. Handy for swapping versions and sharing datasets; if the target is deleted, the link becomes broken.

lnx_env_vars.title: Environment variables (PATH, export)
lnx_env_vars.definition: "Name=value" pairs a process inherits from its parent. export makes a variable visible to child processes; PATH defines where to look for executables.

lnx_nvidia_smi.title: nvidia-smi
lnx_nvidia_smi.definition: An NVIDIA GPU monitoring utility: utilization, used video memory, temperature, and process list. The first thing to check to see who is using the card and how much memory is left.

lnx_disk_usage.title: df and du
lnx_disk_usage.definition: df shows free space on mounted filesystems; du shows how much specific directories take up. The go-to pair for troubleshooting "out of disk space."

lnx_grep.title: grep
lnx_grep.definition: Searches for lines matching a pattern in files and streams. With -r it walks directories, with -i it ignores case, with -n it prints line numbers; the main tool for digging through logs.

lnx_archives.title: tar and gzip
lnx_archives.definition: tar bundles a file tree into a single archive, and gzip compresses it: tar -czf. The standard way to move datasets and checkpoints between machines.

lnx_shell.title: Shell
lnx_shell.definition: The command interpreter between the user and the kernel: bash, zsh, sh. It expands patterns, substitutes variables, builds pipelines, and runs scripts.

git_commit.title: Commit
git_commit.definition: A snapshot of the repository state with an author, a message, and a reference to its parent. Identified by a hash; a project's history is a connected graph of commits.

git_branch.title: Branch
git_branch.definition: A movable pointer to a commit. A branch lets you work in parallel with the main line and bring the work back via merge or rebase.

git_head.title: HEAD
git_head.definition: A pointer to the current position in history, usually the tip of the active branch. HEAD~1 means the previous commit; when you check out a specific commit, HEAD becomes "detached".

git_staging.title: Staging Area (Index)
git_staging.definition: An intermediate area between the working tree and the repository: git add puts changes into the index, and git commit records exactly its contents.

git_working_tree.title: Working Tree
git_working_tree.definition: The project files as they are on disk. git status shows the differences between the working tree, the index, and the last commit.

git_merge.title: Merge
git_merge.definition: Combining the histories of two branches. If the changes do not overlap, a merge commit is created; if they do, Git asks you to resolve the conflict manually.

git_conflict.title: Merge Conflict
git_conflict.definition: A situation where both branches changed the same part of a file and Git cannot pick a version automatically. Resolved manually using the <<<<<<< and >>>>>>> markers.

git_rebase.title: Rebase
git_rebase.definition: Moving a branch's commits onto a different base: history becomes linear, but the commits get new hashes. Not used on branches other people already see.

git_cherry_pick.title: Cherry-pick
git_cherry_pick.definition: Applying one specific commit to the current branch without merging the whole history. Typical for delivering a hotfix to a release branch.

git_squash.title: Squash
git_squash.definition: Collapsing several commits into one during a merge or interactive rebase, so that the main branch gets one meaningful commit instead of a dozen intermediate ones.

git_reflog.title: Reflog
git_reflog.definition: A local log of movements of HEAD and branches. Lets you recover commits after a bad reset or a deleted branch; entries are kept for a limited time.

git_reset_revert.title: reset and revert
git_reset_revert.definition: reset moves a branch back and rewrites history (--soft keeps the changes, --hard discards them); revert creates a new commit that undoes an earlier one without touching history.

git_stash.title: Stash
git_stash.definition: A temporary shelf for uncommitted changes: put them away, switch to another branch, then bring them back with git stash pop.

git_remote.title: Remote Repository (origin, upstream)
git_remote.definition: A copy of the repository on a server. origin is usually your own fork or the main repository; upstream is the original project the fork was made from.

git_fetch_pull.title: fetch and pull
git_fetch_pull.definition: fetch downloads changes from the server without touching your working branches; pull is fetch plus an automatic merge or rebase into the current branch.

git_push.title: Push
git_push.definition: Sending local commits to a remote repository. Push with --force rewrites other people's history, so on shared branches it is replaced with --force-with-lease.

git_clone_fork.title: Clone and Fork
git_clone_fork.definition: clone creates a local copy of a repository with its history; fork is a server-side copy in your own account, from which you then send pull requests to the original project.

git_pull_request.title: Pull Request
git_pull_request.definition: A request to merge a branch into the main one, with discussion, code review, and CI checks. In GitLab the same mechanism is called a merge request.

git_code_review.title: Code Review
git_code_review.definition: Another developer examining changes before they are merged: looking for bugs, simplifications, and deviations from agreed conventions. Discussion happens in pull request comments.

git_diff.title: Diff (Patch)
git_diff.definition: A line-by-line difference between file versions: lines with a minus sign were removed, lines with a plus sign were added. You look at diffs during review and when resolving conflicts.

git_tag_release.title: Tag and Release
git_tag_release.definition: A tag is a fixed label on a commit, usually a version per SemVer. From a tag, GitHub builds a release with release notes and artifacts.

git_gitignore.title: .gitignore
git_gitignore.definition: A list of path patterns Git does not track: virtual environments, caches, model weights, secrets. Ignoring does not remove files that are already committed.

git_lfs.title: Git LFS
git_lfs.definition: An extension for large binary files: the repository stores a pointer, and the file itself lives on a separate server. Otherwise datasets and weights bloat the history forever.

git_flow.title: Git Flow and Trunk-Based Development
git_flow.definition: Two branching models: Git Flow with long-lived develop and release branches versus Trunk-Based with short branches and frequent merges into the main one behind feature flags.

git_protected_branch.title: Protected Branch
git_protected_branch.definition: A repository setting that forbids direct pushes to main: changes go in only through pull requests with mandatory review and green CI checks.

git_gha.title: GitHub Actions
git_gha.definition: GitHub's built-in CI/CD system: a workflow is described in a YAML file under .github/workflows, runs on an event, and executes jobs made of steps on runners.

git_gha_runner.title: Runner
git_gha_runner.definition: The machine that runs a workflow job. It can be GitHub-hosted or self-hosted, for example with your own GPU for training tests.

git_gha_trigger.title: Workflow Trigger (on:)
git_gha_trigger.definition: The event that starts a run: push, pull_request, schedule for cron runs, or workflow_dispatch for a manual button. Path filters save time in a monorepo.

git_gha_reusable.title: Reusable Workflow
git_gha_reusable.definition: A workflow called from other workflows like a function: shared build and test logic is described once and reused across repositories.

git_gha_secrets.title: Secrets and GITHUB_TOKEN
git_gha_secrets.definition: Encrypted values available to a workflow as environment variables. GITHUB_TOKEN is issued automatically for the duration of a run; its permissions are narrowed with the permissions block.

git_gha_badge.title: Status Badge
git_gha_badge.definition: An image in the README showing the result of the latest workflow run. A quick signal that the build and tests on the main branch are green.

mlg_pipeline.title: Pipeline
mlg_pipeline.definition: A chain of automated steps (data collection, preprocessing, training, validation, deployment) that can be reproduced end to end instead of being run manually piece by piece.

mlg_artifact.title: Artifact
mlg_artifact.definition: Any file produced by a pipeline step: model weights, metrics, a preprocessor, a dataset. It is versioned and stored separately so the run can be reproduced.

mlg_feature_store.title: Feature Store
mlg_feature_store.definition: A store of features with a single definition for training and inference. Eliminates training-serving skew: the same logic computes features offline and online.

mlg_drift.title: Data and Model Drift
mlg_drift.definition: Production data diverging from training data (data drift) or a change in the underlying relationship itself (concept drift). Model metrics drop with no code change; caught by monitoring distributions.

mlg_reproducibility.title: Reproducibility
mlg_reproducibility.definition: The ability to get the same result again: pinned versions of data, code, dependencies, and the random seed, plus a saved environment (image, lock file).

mlg_cicd.title: CI/CD
mlg_cicd.definition: Automated build, tests, and deployment on every code change. In ML, data checks, retraining, and model validation before deployment are added.

dock_containerization.title: Containerization
dock_containerization.definition: Packaging an application with all its dependencies into an isolated environment on a shared OS kernel; lighter than a VM, with predictable deployment.

dock_image.title: Docker Image
dock_image.definition: An immutable template of filesystem layers and metadata from which containers are created. Built from a Dockerfile or pulled from a registry.

dock_container.title: Container
dock_container.definition: A running instance of an image with an isolated process, network, and mount points; shares the host kernel.

dock_dockerfile.title: Dockerfile
dock_dockerfile.definition: A declarative build specification: FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, RUN, ENV, EXPOSE, CMD/ENTRYPOINT.

dock_compose.title: Docker Compose
dock_compose.definition: Orchestrating multiple containers on a single host via YAML: services, networks, volumes, startup dependencies.

dock_registry.title: Container Registry
dock_registry.definition: A store of images (Docker Hub, ECR, GCR): versioning, scanning, pulling in CI/CD.

dock_volume.title: Volume / Bind Mount
dock_volume.definition: Persistent data outside the container layer: a named volume or a bind mount of a host directory.

dock_network.title: Docker Networking and Port Publishing
dock_network.definition: Containers talk to each other by service name on a shared bridge network. A port is exposed externally by publishing it with -p host:container; EXPOSE in a Dockerfile only documents it.

k8s_kubernetes.title: Kubernetes
k8s_kubernetes.definition: A container orchestrator: desired state in manifests, a control plane (API Server, etcd, Scheduler, Controller Manager), and worker nodes with kubelet and a container runtime.

k8s_cluster.title: Kubernetes Cluster
k8s_cluster.definition: A set of nodes: the control plane holds the state, workers run Pods; a single API for deployment and scaling.

k8s_pod.title: Pod
k8s_pod.definition: The smallest schedulable unit: one or more co-located containers sharing a network namespace; its IP may change when it is recreated.

k8s_deployment.title: Deployment (Kubernetes)
k8s_deployment.definition: A controller for Pod replicas with rolling updates and rollback; declares the desired number of replicas and the container template.

k8s_service.title: Service
k8s_service.definition: A stable access point to Pods: cluster IP, DNS, load balancing; hides IP changes across restarts.

k8s_etcd.title: etcd
k8s_etcd.definition: A distributed key-value store for Kubernetes cluster configuration and state.

k8s_kubelet.title: kubelet
k8s_kubelet.definition: The agent on a worker node: receives Pod specs from the API and manages the container runtime.

k8s_manifest.title: Kubernetes Manifest
k8s_manifest.definition: A YAML/JSON description of resources (Pod, Service, Deployment): apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec.

k8s_desired_state.title: Desired State
k8s_desired_state.definition: The target state of resources; controllers continuously reconcile the current state toward the desired state.

kfk_topic.title: Topic
kfk_topic.definition: A named event log in Kafka; logically a "channel" or "table" of the stream.

kfk_partition.title: Partition
kfk_partition.definition: A physical shard of a topic: an ordered sequence with its own offsets; consumer group parallelism is limited by the number of partitions.

kfk_offset.title: Offset
kfk_offset.definition: A monotonically increasing position identifier within a partition; a consumer group stores its committed offset to resume reading.

kfk_broker.title: Broker
kfk_broker.definition: A server in a Kafka cluster that stores leader/replica partitions and serves produce/fetch requests.

kfk_producer_consumer.title: Producer / Consumer
kfk_producer_consumer.definition: A producer writes to a topic; a consumer reads from it; a consumer group distributes partitions among its members.

kfk_retention.title: Retention
kfk_retention.definition: The policy for keeping messages by time/size; after the retention period, events are deleted or compacted (log compaction for key-value data).

kfk_delivery_semantics.title: At-most-once / At-least-once / Exactly-once
kfk_delivery_semantics.definition: Delivery guarantees: messages may be lost, duplicated, or processed strictly once (EOS, together with transactions/idempotency on the consumer side).

kfk_schema_registry.title: Schema Registry
kfk_schema_registry.definition: Centralized storage of Avro/Protobuf/JSON Schema schemas with compatibility versioning for producers and consumers.

kfk_connect.title: Kafka Connect
kfk_connect.definition: A framework for integrating sources and sinks (databases, object storage) with Kafka via connectors.

kfk_streams.title: Kafka Streams / ksqlDB
kfk_streams.definition: Stream processing on top of Kafka logs: stateful topologies, windows, tables/changelogs.

prom_counter_gauge.title: Counter and Gauge (Prometheus)
prom_counter_gauge.definition: A Counter only goes up (requests, errors); a Gauge goes both up and down (memory, queue length).

prom_histogram_summary.title: Histogram and Summary
prom_histogram_summary.definition: Histogram: buckets + sum + count, with quantiles computed server-side via histogram_quantile. Summary: quantiles computed client-side, which makes aggregation across replicas difficult.

prom_promql.title: PromQL
prom_promql.definition: The query language for Prometheus time series: selectors, rate(), increase(), aggregations, alerts.

prom_exporter.title: Exporter / scrape
prom_exporter.definition: A component or library that exposes metrics on /metrics; Prometheus periodically scrapes targets according to its configuration.

prom_alertmanager.title: Alertmanager
prom_alertmanager.definition: Routes alerts from Prometheus: deduplication, grouping, integrations with Slack/PagerDuty.

graf_dashboard.title: Grafana Dashboard
graf_dashboard.definition: A set of panels with queries to data sources; its JSON is versioned; used for on-call and drift monitoring.

graf_datasource.title: Data Source
graf_datasource.definition: A connection to Prometheus, Loki, a database, etc.; variables and access permissions are configured at the organization level.

graf_panel_query.title: Panel and Query
graf_panel_query.definition: A visualization of a time series, table, or heatmap; a PromQL or SQL query in the panel editor.

graf_variable.title: Dashboard Variables
graf_variable.definition: Template variables ($instance, $model) for switching a dashboard without duplicating it; cascading is supported.

graf_loki.title: Loki
graf_loki.definition: A log aggregator from Grafana Labs: label indexing plus compressed chunks; paired with Grafana for exploring logs.

clo_iaas_paas_saas.title: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
clo_iaas_paas_saas.definition: IaaS: VMs, networking, disks. PaaS: managed services (databases, k8s). SaaS: ready-made applications. The choice trades control against development speed.

clo_vpc.title: VPC
clo_vpc.definition: An isolated virtual network in the cloud: subnets, routes, firewalls/security groups.

clo_managed_k8s.title: Managed Kubernetes
clo_managed_k8s.definition: EKS/ACK/GKE/Yandex Managed Kubernetes: the provider runs the control plane; you manage the worker nodes and applications.

clo_object_storage.title: Object Storage
clo_object_storage.definition: S3-compatible buckets for artifacts, datasets, and logs; billed by volume and requests.

clo_gpu_instance.title: GPU Instance
clo_gpu_instance.definition: A virtual machine with a GPU, rented by the hour. An expensive line in the bill: savings come from spot instances, auto-stopping idle machines, and moving inference to CPU.

dbs_acid.title: ACID
dbs_acid.definition: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: the properties of transactions in relational DBMSs.

dbs_cap.title: CAP Theorem
dbs_cap.definition: In a distributed system, during network partitions you cannot guarantee both full availability and strong consistency at once; you choose a trade-off (CP/AP).

dbs_sharding.title: Sharding
dbs_sharding.definition: Horizontal partitioning of data by key into independent shards to scale writes.

dbs_replication.title: Replication
dbs_replication.definition: Copies of data on replicas: master-replica, read scaling; synchronous vs. asynchronous replication affects RPO.

dbs_index.title: Database Index
dbs_index.definition: A structure (B-tree, hash) that speeds up lookups and sorting; a trade-off against storage space and write speed.

dbs_nosql.title: NoSQL Families
dbs_nosql.definition: Key-value, document, wide-column, graph: different models for scale and flexible schemas; BASE rather than ACID across the whole cluster.

dbs_transaction.title: Transaction
dbs_transaction.definition: A group of operations executed entirely or not at all: BEGIN, then COMMIT or ROLLBACK. The foundation of ACID guarantees when clients work concurrently.

mlf_tracking.title: MLflow Tracking
mlf_tracking.definition: Logging of parameters, metrics, and artifacts into runs; a UI and API for comparing experiments.

mlf_run.title: Run and Experiment
mlf_run.definition: An experiment groups runs; a run is a single training job with metrics, config, and a code/data version.

mlf_model_registry.title: Model Registry
mlf_model_registry.definition: Model versioning, Staging/Production stages, signatures, and transitions with approval.

mlf_artifact.title: Artifacts
mlf_artifact.definition: Files attached to a run: weights, ONNX, reports; kept in an artifact store (local, S3, GCS).

tb_graph.title: Graph / Profiler
tb_graph.definition: Visualization of the computation graph and per-node profiling for PyTorch/TF.

wb_run_sweep.title: W&B run and sweep
wb_run_sweep.definition: A run logs metrics live; a sweep is a grid/random search or Bayesian optimization of hyperparameters across agents.

wb_artifact_wandb.title: W&B Artifacts
wb_artifact_wandb.definition: Versioning of datasets and models with lineage between artifacts.

clm_experiment_manager.title: ClearML Experiment Manager
clm_experiment_manager.definition: Experiment tracking, automatic artifact capture, comparison, and reproducibility.

clm_agent_orchestration.title: ClearML Agent
clm_agent_orchestration.definition: A worker that pulls tasks from a queue: launches training on compute nodes from the UI/API.
